items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The material for the new band's first album was recorded in November of 1968 and then released by Fontana Records in March of 1969. 1. "Walking in the Park" (3:51) the effects of the band members' Blues/R&B "training" is very evident with their choice to cover this Graham Bond song: from its opening bass riff the structure is rooted solidly in the Blues traditions. Where the band shows Jazz influences are in David Greenslade's organ play, Jon Hiseman's very active and surprisingly creative use of syncopation and machine gun fills, as well as the volume of the "horn section" of Henry Lowther and Dick Heckstall-Smith. James Litherland's vocal is great but it's more the presence of that gravelly male voice that reminds us of the heavier musical styles forming and erupting in the late 1960s. There's a lot of work to do before a higher quality of sound engineering and the band members' individual styles blend together in the cohesive style that is to come, but the talent is definitely on full display! (9/10)2. "Plenty Hard Luck" (4:23) another blues form over which Dave and Jon put on a clinic of Cream- and Argent-like Power Rock while Dick and the rest of the band seem to lag a bit "behind" in the rudiments of the Blues World. James Litherland's vocal seems of secondary importance--and he struggles a bit to deliver lead guitar on a level anywhere near Jon, Dick, and Dave's. As the song opens with a fade in (from a previously-established jam) it is no surprise that the song's compositional credit goes to the whole band. Busy Jon Hiseman is a little overpowering of the overall music--especially when Tony and James are playing in such safe and rudimentary Blues territory. Toward the very end the band's overall sound seems to finally begin to blend better. (8.667/10)3. "Mandarin" (4:27) an instrumental that quickly makes room for Tony Reeves to display his bass skills with an unusually-unaccompanied and -long (over 90 seconds) solo. When Jon rejoins in the middle of the third minute Tony clicks on the wah-wah effect, turns up the volume a bit, and continues . . . until 3:40! A gong crash signals the return of the full band into a form and palette that seems totally new and previously un-introduced (which leads me to believe that this song's four and a half minutes was excerpted from a much longer jam--one that started with the whole band motif that is displayed here at the end). In all honestly, Tony is not a very impressive (or even good) bass player--even with the effects turned on! But I would have loved to hear more of the whole band jam that was allowed to come through at the very end! (8.25/10) 4. "Debut" (6:20) another song founded on a Blues structure, this one, unfortunately, puts some disappointing restrictions on Jon Hiseman's drumming--which diminishes the quality of both his performance and the song, overall. Solos from Dick and Dave are fine enough (Dave is actually quite a fine organist--very creative and not afraid to use odd/new effects), but over this rather dull and dated foundation it just doesn't have any staying power. And then, unfortunately, plugging James' lead guitar into the mix (at the very end!) does nothing to improve the song or palette. (8.667/10) 5. "Beware the Ides of March" (5:34) a clear nod (and rather blatant take on the PROCOL HARUM monster hit--the slow dance of the decade: "A Whiter Shade of Pale"), it does allow plenty of room for Jon to impress (and, boy! does he!), Dick to add his own creative , as well as Dave to show off his advanced organ skills--as well as some cool piano & harpsichord after the 2:20 shift, before the band's ramp up in the fourth minute into a hard-driving, fast-paced Power Rock motif with James Litherland's loud but fitting lead guitar and the rest of the band's frenzied, frenetic letting-loose play up to the 4:52 mark. Great stuff! A real album highlight for me. But then they return to the sax-led "Whiter Shade" motif to close things out. Rated up for that amazing middle section (as well as for Dave and Jon's creative skills displays). (9/10)6. "The Road She Walked Before" (2:39) this bluesy R&B tune from Dick Heckstall-Smith leans much more into both recent Jazz and R&B traditions that had proved successful in the Pop World (with artists like Dave Brubeck, Ray Charles, and Herbie Hancock). I really like this one (as it is far less blues-based). It is, interestingly, the album's only composition attributed to a single member of the band. (9/10)7. "Backwater Blues" (7:35) yes, we're definitely reverting to the Blues--the Deep Southern Blues of the Mississippi-Louisiana Bayou juke joints. I have to admit that James Litherland's excellent here vocals the early performances of Rod Stewart and Robert Plant--and the guest appearance of guitarist Jim Roche on lead guitar was definitely a stroke of genius. Both Tony Reeves and Dick Heckstall-Smith really excel: confirming some tremendous talent at playing the blues; Tony is so disciplined, so precise, and Dick is amazing at expressing the Blues to its absolute limits with both of his saxes (first tenor, then soprano, then two tracks merged together!) Very cool. I don't normally like the Blues much but I cannot help but extol the performances here. This is a great rendering of some classic Blues--the only "flaw" in the sound palette might be Jon Hiseman's too Jazz-flashy drumming! (14/15) 8. "Those About to Die" (4:49) a very spirited song that features some rather astonishing organ work from Dave Greenslade and some very interesting thematic shifts in the composition. Solos in this instrumental also appear from Dick and James, but it's Dave that really rises above the crop. Once again Jon's busy drum work feels a little too Tony Williams-jazzy/busy--which, unfortunately, is not befitting of the song's over all vibe. (8.875/10)Total Time 39:38 B/four stars; an excellent debut album that shows a band of Blues-trained musicians hell-bent on making something more vibrant and dynamic than their past bands--more on the level of Cream, Argent, or even Procol Harum. Also, I don't know if the songs were ordered on the album in the chronology of their creation, but the band does seem to show signs of gelling better the further the album progresses--which is also born out with their successive work on Jack Bruce's album as well as their own sophomore release, Valentyne Suite.

items.body: Review by octopus-4 — There's not much that can be said about this last Roz Vitalis album: it's a compilation of tracks spanning all the 25 years of the band's activity.Of course many albums are not represented in the tracklist, Roz Vitalis have a huge output even taking into account that many of their over 40 albums are live.One thing to say is that the actual lineup doesn't feature some of the historical band members, but the replacemets work very well, also because in all the incarnations they are mainly supporting the creative genius of Ivan Rozmainsky.Despite being a live recording, part of the tracks have almost a studio quality. Only on Premonitions (track 6) there is some noisy distortion. Wrong recording volumes, on the heavy guitar. I don't know which guitar is being used, but I've heard a similar sound when I used distortion on very old electri guitars. So likely a technical issue, not a lack of skill.The instruments sound a little out of tune in the following track, but it's the flute that sounds not well "tempered". These two "defects" tell us that this is real music. The guitar noise could have been removed in post-production, but not having done it is a "plus" for me. Let me draw an example: the concert of The Wall in Berlin was a disaster, but the post production adjusted many of its faults. As a result we have an album that can't be considered an effective document of that night.This Roz Vitalis live is genuine. Not correcting the tracks in post production tells us how exactly a Roz Vitalis concert can sound, and considering that for me attending at one of their gigs is very unlikely, I'm happy to hear their real sound.For who is already in their sympho-avant-prog, it's a good live with an interesting choice of tracks. For who is new to Roz Vitalis this can be a starting point as well as the live at the Christ Church Cathedral has been for Clannad.Note: this is a name your price release on Bandcamp.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — As a tender 22 year old female multi-instrumentalist, JOANNA NEWSOM was already arm wrestling with the big boys when "The Milk Eyed Mender" appeared, though it took next year's "Ys" for the audience to catch up. This is to say nothing of her wildly voice somewhere between MS KATE B, IRIS DEMENT and Nanna Brynd�s Hilmarsd�ttir of OF MONSTERS AND MEN with perhaps a spousal affiliation to one of David Seville's chipmunks, take your pick whom if you even know what I'm talking about. Apart from the at times luscious harps and etymologically allied keyboards augmenting sometimes surprisingly conventional melodies, it's really her voice and only occasionally decipherable lyrics (and that's when you can even discern them) that propels these numbers. She might cite ROY HARPER as a favorite artist and doubtless influence, but it's COLIN MELOY of the contemporaneous DECEMBERISTS who seems the biggest benefactor of her curious phrasings in some of the best tracks here, like "Bridges and Balloons" and "En Gallop". For variety and endearingly kooky rants, give "Inflammatory Writ" and "Peach Plum Pear" a dozen of so spins before you realize what you are up against. Don't pass up the Appalachia infused "Three Little Babes" or the jazzy "Book of Right On" either.I'm told some vocal changes a decade or so hence made later versions of these flowing gems more palatable, but I'm not even sure what that means when it comes to Joanna, or even whether that's a good thing. But this is all at least unwittingly addictive and at most congenial genius, even if it doesn't quite hit enough highs to offset the averages, and a debut that's more raw than homogenized.

items.body: Cosmic producers and acclaimed record collectors Psychemagik have proved that they know how to get their hands dirty and dig out the obscure and unusual to pull an interesting compilation together. One half of the Psychemagik duo, Skyrager (aka Danny McLewin) has done the business again on a brand new comp for Mr Bongo titled ‘Coconut Dreams’. An eclectic, widescreen soundtrack to a mythical utopia where everything is just groovy, the tracklist wanders from tripped out ambience and stark electro-reggae to cosmic folk-soul like this rare early ‘70s beauty from Joseph (Millar). Near enough impossible to find an original copy of the 7 inch these days, 'Three O'Clock In The Morning' is a transcendent slice of jazz-infused folk-soul that burns with energy and good vibes. With an intro of acoustic guitar and congas that explodes into a funky, brass-heavy whirlwind, the (too short) song is reminiscent of Terry Callier at full throttle, Joseph’s extraordinary vocals soaring like a purer-toned version of Tim Buckley at his horniest (as in brass instrument influenced). What a tune! ‘Coconut Dreams’ is released on Mr Bongo on September 4th 2026!

items.body: Rafał Blechacz’s recent release is, in his own words, a continuation of an earlier project he recorded for DG back in 2008, an album of sonatas by Haydn, Beethoven, and Mozart. The unifying motif of this new chapter, in part a collaboration with Kent Nagano and the Dresdner Philharmonie, is the key of C minor: a key whose emotional weight Blechacz finds significant. Piano Concertos Amazon Presto Apple Mozart‘s Piano Concerto No. 24 is one of just two minor-key concertos in his entire catalogue, and its stormy drama looks ahead to Beethoven. Where the No. 20 in D minor is arguably more fiery, the C minor carries a distinct gravitas. This reading expresses the solemnity clearly but also taps into the drama, as we hear in the orchestral introduction of the Allegro (track 1). The Dresdner ensemble has a nicely blended, resonant sound, but the rousing nature of the orchestral parts calls for the raw horn blasts of Leif Ove Andsnes’s version with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra (Sony, 2022) or the angular urgency of Jean-Efflam Bavouzet’s with the Manchester Camerata under Gábor Takács-Nagy (Chandos, 2023). Blechacz’s tone is lithe, vocal, and silky, highlighting the elegance of Mozart’s arching phrases. I found it too uniform in personality, however. The second theme, as an example, is far too placid where it could use more texture and zest. The Larghetto (track 2) offers some of Mozart’s most exquisite orchestral writing, highlighting the best timbres of each instrument. Once again, the ensemble proves well integrated, but I wished for more distinctive character, especially between winds and strings, a quality that comes through better in Mitsuko Uchida’s earlier version with Jeffrey Tate and the English Chamber Orchestra (Philips, 1989). Her noticeably slower tempo underscores a more deliberate, individual reading. Beethoven‘s C minor Concerto marks the transition between his early and middle periods: we hear elements of Classical elegance alongside the heroic character of his middle-period works to come. The orchestra lays a strong foundation in its extended introduction. Blechacz is most eloquent in the melodious moments, and there are some lovely color changes throughout. Yet when it comes to generating a more substantial presence, things feel mismatched against the orchestra’s power. The cadenza is a good example: I kept waiting for him to tap into that quintessentially Beethovenian urgency, drive, and ‘madness,’ but was left a bit disappointed by the relative tameness of the solo. There is much to savor in the gentle glow Blechacz gives the E major key of the Largo (track 5). The opening needs more profundity (sample Leon Fleisher with George Szell), but the running discourse with the orchestra is nicely rendered: the piano may be too heavily miked from 3’30” onwards, yet we still hear the interchanging woodwinds float beautifully above the gently rolling arpeggios. In the finale, the signature offbeat accents would benefit from more sharpness, but the jauntiness of the rondo is still there, and the orchestra again comes through with barreling energy in its interludes. Rafał Blechacz. Photo © Marco Borggreve. The solo offering, Beethoven’s 32 Variations, WoO 80, closes the album with remarkable clarity. Blechacz’s agility is on full display, his nimble passagework expertly outlining Beethoven’s intricate counterpoint. While the reading is energetic, with pointed, crisp staccatos, it feels light-handed, missing a bigger, more orchestral sound. There could also be more variety across sections, notably the C major variations (tracks 11–12). While they exude an appropriate feeling of peace, they never quite register as a true arrival. For more sonorous dimension, turn to Uchida’s version (Philips, 1999) and to Glenn Gould’s from 1970, memorable for its unmistakable obstinacy. Blechacz’s strong suit has always lain in his reading of the finest nuances, but that vision feels rather muted on this album, partly because these works are so inherently dramatic and call for a different approach. Primary recommendations remain unchanged. items.body: New York synthwave duo Bunny X released the video for “Even If We Don’t Talk” on 24 August 2026. The track sits fourth on “Love On A High Floor”, the duo’s third album, which Aztec Records issued on 14 August 2026. Abigail Gordon and Jenny Bates sing over a synth-driven arrangement that mixes Italo disco pulse with mid-tempo synthwave. Alice Teeple directed the video, with Bates handling the visual effects. Parts of it were filmed around New York’s Financial District, and the story turns a sequence of missed meetings into comedy set in an eighties office. Gordon points to how late the song arrived in the album sessions. “This track was a latecomer in the writing process and almost didn’t make the final cut at all since album production was in the final stages by the time the idea for the song came about,” she said. “Even If We Don’t Talk”, she added, “explores the lingering inability to move on from a past love and the hope that something might still happen.” Teeple set out the visual references she worked from. “We wanted to make this look as authentically from the 80s as possible,” she said. She named the television series “Moonlighting”, the film “9-5” and “The Twilight Zone”, along with The Boomtown Rats video for “Banana Republic”, then described the plot device: “I loved the idea of missed connections due to transit troubles, crossed wires, and rotten timing.” What is on the Bunny X album ‘Love On A High Floor’ “Love On A High Floor” runs eleven tracks. The order is “Starting Dreams”, “True Confession”, “One Touch”, “Even If We Don’t Talk”, “After Hours”, “Take Me Away”, “Night Moves”, “Love On A High Floor”, “Believe In You”, “Business Trip” and “Lovers”. The album returns to the characters of the 2021 debut “Young & In Love” and follows them into offices, cocktail bars and late taxi rides set against 1980s Wall Street. Gordon and Bates wrote the album with a rotating set of collaborators. John Bourke, who records as Gosteffects, co-wrote and produced eight tracks. Kevin Montgomery of SelloRekt / LA Dreams co-wrote and produced five, and three of the album’s songs began as his instrumentals. David Petterson, who records as Don Dellpiero, worked on the opener. Tony Lake and Chip Cosby contributed to further tracks. Guest performers run through the second half. Mary Hanley, who co-founded the duo, sings on “One Touch”. Cosby, of Heartracer, plays the guitar lead on “After Hours”, and Lake takes the solo on “Take Me Away”. Emma Ballentine Dykes and Darryn McHardie of The Lightning Kids appear on the closing track “Lovers”. Kelli McGuire shot the album photography. Andrew B. White handled design and layout. The album is out digitally and on Bandcamp, with vinyl, CD and cassette editions pressed to order through Elastic Stage. Love On A High Floor by Bunny X About Bunny X Bunny X formed in New York City around Abigail Gordon and Mary Hanley as an Italo disco and Hi-NRG project. Their first release under the name, the single “Berlin, in December”, appeared on 1 May 2013, written and produced by Conrad Kaneshiro with Gordon and Hanley co-writing and performing. Kaneshiro stayed a regular collaborator through the pair’s early singles, among them “Hit Show”, “Stay” and “If You Say Yes”. A run of collaborations with other producers followed. The duo recorded “NYC Sunrise” with Marvel83′, “If You Say Goodbye” with Driver86, “Strangers Again” with Syntronix and “Try Again” with Mondmann. Further joint tracks came with Zak Vortex, Oblique and Thought Beings. The seven-track EP “We Demand Fun” arrived on 15 March 2019. The first album, “Young & In Love”, came out on 5 October 2021 through Aztec Records, ten tracks built on teenage romance and first crushes. A remix edition and instrumental versions followed. The second album, “Love Minus 80”, arrived on 26 May 2023 with nine tracks and also produced a remix set, alongside standalone reworks by Cassetter and Earmake. The six-track EP “Never Give You Up” came on 3 April 2025. Hanley stepped back from the line-up for medical reasons and Jenny Bates joined Gordon, the pairing that made “Love On A High Floor”. Bates also handles the duo’s visual effects work, including the video for “Even If We Don’t Talk”.

items.body: Mousecunt, an anonymous three-piece from Iran, release their nine-track album “Orgasmic Mouse” on September 25, 2026. It is the first release on Infibulate Records, a new label that trades only in Monero and does not require its artists to disclose their legal identities. The band mix deathrock, gothic rock, punk-metal and sparse synth-led post-punk across the record, which is told through an unreliable narrator who shifts between identities, ages and perspectives, sometimes accuser and sometimes accused. The Mousecunt album was cut in a two-week session at a private studio in Azerbaijan in 2026. The label credits a Nord synthesiser and vocals to one member, Gibson guitar, Höfner bass and vocals to a second, and Tama drums to a third; an anonymous engineer in the United States handled mixing and mastering. Track five, “The Orgasming”, is streaming now from the label’s own page; the remaining eight open on release day. The running order is “Fucking the Mirror”, “W*man’s Eyes”, “You Know About Art?”, “Mom Too”, “The Orgasming”, “Your Repulsive Husband”, “Godspeed”, “Cunt” and “Pornography ’97-’26”. A cassette edition runs to thirty hand-numbered copies on black shells, each marked with different hand-drawn artwork. Pre-orders open on September 15, 2026 at USD 35, with advance orders dispatched on September 18 and later orders within three days. A lossless digital edition in WAV and FLAC follows on release day at USD 10. Both are sold directly and paid in Monero; the label describes its shop as a “Monero-only store […] Limited handmade cassette editions and lossless digital releases sold directly without cards, PayPal or third-party checkout”. “Orgasmic Mouse” has no Bandcamp, Spotify, YouTube or Discogs presence, so the label’s own page is the only confirmed point of access. About Mousecunt Mousecunt formed in Iran in 2022 and, by the label’s account, spent its early years making private recordings and giving unannounced performances. The three members are not named. Nothing has been issued publicly under the name before “Orgasmic Mouse”, and the band has no presence on the usual streaming, retail or discography platforms. Infibulate Records is equally new. The label describes itself as an anonymous operation for artists making “abrasive, obscene and uncompromising work”, releasing digitally, assembling cassettes and small-run objects by hand, and selling directly for Monero rather than through card, PayPal or third-party checkout. It states that it accepts demos, collaborations, split releases and live proposals. “Orgasmic Mouse” carries the catalogue number SEW-001 and is the label’s opening release.

It covers Williams’ work as musician, poet and visual artist, his role in founding Christian Death and his part in shaping the sound and imagery of Los Angeles deathrock. Who plays the Pomona concert The performance brings together original Christian Death players Rikk Agnew on guitar, James McGearty on bass and David Glass on drums, with vocals from Eva O, Gitane Demone, Patrik Mata of Kommunity FK, William Faith of Shadow Project and Kenton Holmes. The set draws on the albums “Only Theatre of Pain”, “Catastrophe Ballet” and “Ashes”, extended with Shadow Project material. Nico B told Side-Line the film’s European premiere is set for the Entrange Festival in Belgium on September 7 and 12. Two trailers are online, “Angel” and “Demon“. About Rozz Williams Rozz Williams was born Roger Alan Painter on November 6, 1963 and formed Christian Death in Southern California in 1979. The band’s 1982 debut “Only Theatre of Pain” set much of the template for American deathrock and fed into the gothic rock scenes on both sides of the Atlantic. Williams distanced himself from the goth label through the 1980s and 1990s and moved through punk rock, hard rock, cabaret and spoken word instead. Alongside Christian Death he led Shadow Project with Eva O, ran the industrial project Premature Ejaculation, and worked under the names Daucus Karota, Heltir, EXP and Bloodflag. He recorded a series of solo albums and collaborated with Gitane Demone between 1995 and 1996, including the album “Dream Home Heartache”, produced by Nico B. He also painted, wrote poetry and made collage work. Williams died on April 1, 1998 at the age of 34. Nico B founded Cult Videotheek and Cult Epics in Amsterdam in 1991 and knew Williams from the years he lived with Gitane Demone there. The two co-directed the 1998 experimental short film “Pig”, which Williams scored and starred in and which was his last completed work. Nico B went on to publish “The Art of Rozz Williams: From Christian Death to Death” in 1999 and the Edward Colver photography book “Christian Death – Only Theatre of Pain” in 2022. “Rozz Williams: Romeo’s Distress” is his first feature-length film about Williams, released in selected theaters through 2026.

items.body: End-Tek is a side project of ‘Mortum’, better known for his work under the Human Vault moniker. Under the End-Tek name, he has released several albums, including “Mortal Sequence”, which originally appeared in 2020 as a limited cassette release through No Labels Interested. Due to its limited availability, the album remained largely unknown to a wider audience, but it is now receiving a well-deserved second life thanks to Aliens Production. “Mortal Sequence” sounds like Electro music crafted in a synth laboratory. Musically, it is a collection—and, above all, a fusion—of diverse influences, ranging from Industrial and Cinematic sounds to Experimental music and IDM, while remaining firmly rooted in Electro. Despite this broad range of influences, the album feels remarkably cohesive. The compositions are characterized by powerful sounds, extensive manipulation, various effects and, above all, a dark atmosphere. The tracks are primarily instrumental, perfectly complementing the mood and overall style of the album. The record contains some brilliant tracks waiting to be discovered. I particularly recommend the second half, which reveals some incredibly intelligent compositions. Traces of a Mortal Constraint influence can also be detected here and there. It would have been a shame for this album to fade into obscurity. Moreover, this release offers an excellent opportunity to (re)discover End-Tek. (Rating:7½). Aliens Production issued the digital edition on May 12, 2026. It holds nine tracks, opening with “Re-Arranging Happiness” and closing with a second version of that title. Listen to “Dead Kultur”: Dead Kultur by End-Tek About End-Tek End-Tek is the side project of the producer known as Mortum, who also records as Human Vault. The label states that the End-Tek name has been in use since 2005. A first studio album followed in 2008, after which the project stayed inactive for several years, and a second album appeared in 2016. “Mortal Sequence” was completed in 2019 and reached only a short-run cassette edition, which sold out; the audio was not made available digitally at the time. Aliens Production describes the recording as built roughly 80 percent on hardware rather than modern DAW processing. The Slovakian label also issued the End-Tek EP “Two Poles” in 2023. Under the Human Vault name, Mortum has worked with the same label on the remix album “Carnal Motives” and the album “Fragment Existence”. He discussed his approach to writing in a Click Interview with Human Vault. The 2026 digital edition of “Mortal Sequence” now makes the third End-Tek album available outside its original cassette run.

items.body: Unter Strøm, the electronic duo of Alex Gonzales (Matte Blvck) and John Kunkel (The New Division, John Grand), release the single “Stumbling” on August 28, 2026 via Breathing Records. It is the fourth and closing piece of “Between Forms”, the four-single run that also holds “Orynth”, “Fold” and “Fragment”. The track moves through shifting arpeggios and evolving rhythms while keeping a club pulse underneath. Breathing Records describes it as the point where the duo sound “most atmospheric and emotionally exposed.” How Unter Strøm wrote ‘Stumbling’ in a single afternoon “Stumbling” came out of an afternoon that had not been set aside as a writing session. A new project was opened, an arpeggio arrived, a rhythm followed, and most of the record took shape within a few hours. Gonzales and Kunkel expected to return to it later and, by their own account, barely did. The session stayed as it was recorded. Aaron Short mixed the track, continuing the working relationship that runs across the earlier “Between Forms” singles. The duo have described the four records as unlike one another rather than variations on a formula, chosen to mark out the range of the project instead of settling it. That choice put “Stumbling” last in the sequence. About Unter Strøm Unter Strøm is an electronic duo formed by Alex Gonzales and John Kunkel, working between Los Angeles and San Diego after years of playing together in earlier bands and studios. Gonzales also leads the San Diego darkwave and industrial project Matte Blvck, whose singles include “Pupula Duplex” and “Soulless”. Kunkel is the Los Angeles producer behind The New Division, is part of the Los Angeles group Trade Secrets, and produces melodic house as John Grand. The duo debuted in 2025 with the two-track single “Breathing”, then moved to Breathing Records, the label that launched with the “Inhale Vol. I” compilation in November 2025. “Orynth” followed on May 15, 2026, “Fold” on June 12, 2026 and “Fragment” on July 24, 2026, all mixed by Aaron Short. “Stumbling”, out August 28, 2026, ends that sequence and, according to the duo, points toward a body of unreleased material still to come.

items.body: Projekt returns Aurelio Voltaire‘s 1998 debut “The Devil’s Bris” to print on September 11, 2026. The gothic and dark cabaret album comes back as a CD in a 4-panel digipak, in an edition of 300, and is the first pressing in three years. It uses the 2020 remaster, taken from the original mixdown DAT. The twelve-track album carries “When You’re Evil” and “Ex Lover’s Lover”, the two Voltaire songs that have held the longest club life. Projekt describes the record as “this strange brew of gypsy violins, driving rhythms, sardonic wit and turn-of-the-century mayhem.” The Devil's Bris (2020 remaster) by Aurelio Voltaire What ‘The Devil’s Bris’ contains The running order is “Ex Lover’s Lover”, “Anniversary”, “Parade”, “The Man Upstairs”, “They Know Me”, “Oweee”, “Snakes”, “Ravens Land”, “The Chosen”, “All The Way Down”, “When You’re Evil” and “Shalom”, closing on a reading of the Klezmer standard. The arrangements lean on violin, cello and acoustic guitar rather than synthesizers, set against lyrics about love, loss, revenge and dismemberment. The 2020 remaster has already appeared on CD in a run of 500 in March 2021 and on vinyl in two pressings, the first limited to 500 on orange and black swirled vinyl and the second to 300 on orange with red marble. Both have since sold out, and the album has been streaming only in the interim. The September 2026 CD is available through Projekt and Bandcamp. About Aurelio Voltaire Aurelio Voltaire is a New York-based singer and songwriter who also works as an animator, comic book creator and toy designer. He emerged from the New York goth scene of the 1990s and signed to Projekt, the label founded by Sam Rosenthal, which released “The Devil’s Bris” as his debut in 1998 in a jewel case, followed by a 2011 deluxe digipak edition with an eight-page lyric booklet and signed art card. He has recorded and toured for close to three decades across twelve full-length studio albums, among them “Almost Human” and “Heart-Shaped Wound”, both also on Projekt. His songs “Brains!” and “Land of the Dead” were written for the Cartoon Network series “The Grim Adventures of Billy and Mandy”, and his live sets mix murder ballads with science-fiction comedy songs aimed at convention audiences. The September 11, 2026 CD marks the first time “The Devil’s Bris” has been available as a new physical pressing since 2023.

items.body: Duophonic Noise Construction, the dark electro project of X Marks The Pedwalk mastermind Sevren Ni-Arb and his son LMX, release “Abattoir (new version)” on October 23, 2026 through meshwork music. The digital single is a one-track rework of the X Marks The Pedwalk track first issued as a single in 1990 on Zoth Ommog. The rework keeps the aggressive, dark character of the 1990 recording and adds new basslines. Restored samples lifted from the original recording sit inside the new production, and Sevren Ni-Arb again handles the vocals. meshwork music describes the result as “a fusion of modern, hard-hitting cyber-industrial and the untamed fury of the early 90s.” Abattoir (new version) by Duophonic Noise Construction Sevren Ni-Arb returns to a track he first released in 1990 “Abattoir” dates from the period when X Marks The Pedwalk recorded for Zoth Ommog, the Frankfurt label that carried much of the German electro-industrial output of the early 1990s. Rather than reissuing the original, Sevren Ni-Arb has rebuilt the track with his son, who records solo as LMX and whose own albums Sevren has produced from the start. The label points to the lyric as the reason for revisiting it, describing the 1990 text as “a dark dystopian vision” that “reads today almost like a commentary on the present.” The single follows “Cage Dreaming”, released earlier in 2026, and continues a run that began with the digital singles “Always” and “Trauma” in autumn 2024 and the eleven-track album “Distorted Reality” in April 2025. Side-Line spoke to father and son about that working relationship in the Duophonic Noise Construction interview. About Duophonic Noise Construction Duophonic Noise Construction is a German dark electro and industrial duo formed by Sevren Ni-Arb and his son, who records under the name LMX. Sevren Ni-Arb has led X Marks The Pedwalk since 1988 and founded the label meshwork music in 2016, which has issued the X Marks The Pedwalk albums “Superstition” (2023) and “Insomnia” (2025) as well as LMX’s solo work, including “Habits & Addictions” in 2022. The joint project began after Sevren proposed the name and produced artwork for it; LMX answered with the first song sketches. The duo debuted with the digital single “Always” in September 2024, followed by “Trauma” in October 2024 and the album “Distorted Reality” on April 24, 2025. Side-Line covered that album on its announcement and interviewed the pair in July 2025. Sevren Ni-Arb also discussed the parallel X Marks The Pedwalk catalogue in a 2026 Side-Line interview. “Abattoir (new version)”, out October 23, 2026, is the first Duophonic Noise Construction release to draw directly on the X Marks The Pedwalk back catalogue.

items.body: It would be easy to describe Santur & Kamancheh for Electronics as an encounter between Iranian classical instruments and electroacoustic music. Fortunately, that is not what this album is about. Rather than treating tradition and experimentation as opposing worlds, Maryam Rahmani & David Esser allow them to coexist within the same acoustic space. The santur and kamancheh are never presented as historical artefacts awaiting electronic transformation. Instead, electronics become another way of listening to them. From the opening “Glass Tower,” one has the impression that the listener has been placed inside the instruments themselves. Contact microphones, geophones and live processing reveal vibrations that normally remain hidden: the resonance of wood, sympathetic strings, tiny mechanical noises and the physical behaviour of the instruments’ bodies. At times Esser’s electronics recede almost completely, becoming practically undetectable as they simply extend the instruments’ natural resonance, making it difficult to determine where acoustic sound ends and electronic sound begins. This shift in perspective shapes the entire album. “Noah’s Sea Cave” explores darker, more enclosed resonances, but it also introduces one of the record’s most beautiful timbral contrasts. Rahmani’s voice radiates a quiet luminosity that seems to suspend the music from within. Set against the rough physical friction of the santur, it softens the texture without diminishing its material presence. “Copper Playground” shifts the focus towards the kamancheh, whose sustained, vocal quality becomes inseparable from processed field recordings captured in a children’s playground. Rather than functioning as background ambience, these environmental sounds become integral to the musical texture, blurring the distinction between instrument, place and electronics. “Dämmerung” becomes an exercise in gradual disappearance, with instrumental identities dissolving into sustained harmonic fields, while “Fields of Grain” strips the language back to a handful of carefully placed gestures whose expressive force depends entirely on duration and silence. The closing “Bazar of Fireflies” places Rahmani’s luminous gestures within one of the album’s richest electronic environments. Her flickering sonorities continually emerge from a shifting electronic haze, preserving the intimacy of the acoustic instruments even as the electronics become increasingly present. One of the record’s greatest strengths is that it never exoticises its materials. The Persian modal language remains present throughout, but it is never presented as a marker of cultural difference. Equally, the electronics avoid the familiar rhetoric of technological innovation. Both become part of the same musical vocabulary. The dialogue between Rahmani’s santur, kamancheh and voice, and Esser’s electroacoustic practice feels natural, not because their differences disappear, but because each continually reshapes the other’s way of listening. That sense of discovery extends to the album’s construction. Much of the material originated through improvisation before being carefully assembled in the studio into more composed forms. One can hear both processes throughout the record. The music retains the openness and unpredictability of spontaneous performance, yet every track displays a strong sense of formal balance. Nothing feels accidental, even when individual gestures seem to emerge almost by chance. Rather than altering the identity of the instruments, Rahmani and Esser invite us to hear them from a different perspective. photo by Yuulia Vlaskina To find out more about the production process we reached out directly to Maryam Rahmani & David Esser. Santur & Kamancheh for Electronics places two instruments deeply associated with Iranian classical music into a very different sonic environment of contact microphones, geophones, field recordings, and live electronic processing. Rather than presenting tradition and experimentation as opposites, the album seems to allow them to coexist within the same acoustic space. How did the project begin, and at what point did you realise that the Santur and Kamancheh could be transformed in these ways without losing their cultural and emotional identity? Maryam & David: We met 2025 at a concert in Berlin’s Km28 over a Beer and decided to get together for a music session. What began with sharing a meal, memories, and stories naturally evolved into making music. From the very beginning, we encouraged each other to experiment freely with the instruments, without explaining or instructing one another on how to play them. Instead, we allowed the music itself to become our conversation. By listening closely and responding intuitively, we communicated through sound rather than words. The electronic elements were never intended as mere decoration or an addition to the music. They were an essential part of the dialogue, expanding the instruments’ voices and deepening the interaction between us. What became clear quite early in the process was that the identity of the Santur and Kamancheh did not disappear through transformation. Their cultural and emotional presence remained because it was carried by the way they were played, listened to, and responded to. The electronics did not replace that identity-they revealed other dimensions of it. The use of contact microphones and geophones reveals aspects of the instruments that listeners would rarely hear—the vibrations of wood, strings, bodies, and even the surrounding space. Pieces such as “Glass Tower” and “Copper Playground” often feel as though we are listening from inside the instruments rather than outside them. What drew you to these recording techniques, and did hearing the instruments at such a microscopic level change your relationship to them as performers and listeners? Maryam & David: We wanted to change the perspective from which these instruments are usually perceived. Normally, they are heard from a certain distance, but with this album we wanted to place the listener much closer-to move inside the instruments themselves. We wanted to explore their essence without completely distorting them, keeping their character alive while allowing it to be modulated in different ways. In that sense, the instruments became an object of listening, almost like acoustic spaces in themselves. Maryam: Through this way of microphoning, I heard completely different sounds coming from my own instruments. That changed the way I played and responded. Every gesture became different because I was reacting to details that I had never been able to hear before. David: I was fascinated by revealing sonic qualities that are usually considered non-musical-the vibrations of the wood, the body of the instrument, and all the hidden resonances. Ironically, this made me think about sound itself in a much more musical way. Listening at such a microscopic level changed my relationship to the instruments because they became places to explore rather than simply instruments to record. The liner notes describe the album as emerging from experiences of migration, linguistic displacement, and cultural translation, suggesting that sound can carry meanings that language sometimes cannot. Maryam, as an Iranian musician living in Australia, and David, working in Berlin with a strong interest in place and listening, did you find yourselves approaching these themes differently? How did your respective experiences of geography, language, and belonging shape the dialogue between the acoustic instruments and the electronic processing? David: For me, the perception of sound is always connected to memory. In my field recording practice, I search for hidden vibrations within structures and environments. Working with Santur and Kamancheh extended this way of listening into a musical context. The instruments gradually became resonant bodies rather than fixed musical objects. What interested me was not changing their identity, but uncovering layers that usually remain unheard, allowing them to be experienced from a different perspective. Maryam: For me, it often felt like hearing my own reflection through a different world. There were moments when I found myself trying to sound closer to the musical language that felt familiar to me, and other moments when I almost disappeared into this new sonic environment. Over time, I stopped thinking of those experiences as opposites. Instead, I became interested in being fully present with my surroundings while still holding onto my own voice. That shaped the way I approached the dialogue between the Santur and the electronics. I wasn’t trying to preserve one identity or transform into another, but to let both worlds affect each other. The electronics didn’t feel like something separate from the acoustic instrument; they became another space for listening, responding, and discovering how my musical language could exist in a new context without losing where it comes from. A significant part of the material developed through live performance and improvisation, particularly during the 2025 concert at Kühlspot Social Club in Berlin. Tracks such as “Noah’s Sea Cave,” “Fields of Grain,” and “Bazar of Fireflies” feel suspended between composition, memory, and spontaneous discovery. How much of the album emerged from structured ideas and how much from trusting the moment? And do you see this project as the beginning of an ongoing collaboration that may further explore the intersection of Iranian musical traditions, sound art, and electroacoustic experimentation? Maryam & David: All of the music developed through improvisation. We often began with simple sonic ideas, particular recording techniques, or a shared atmosphere rather than fixed compositions. Later in the Studios we combine all the Recordings into a more composed Form. The live performances, especially in Berlin, became an important space for discovering how the acoustic instruments and electronics could respond to one another in real time. Many moments that ended up on the album could never have been planned-they emerged simply through attentive listening, trust, and a willingness to follow the music wherever it led. A key aspect of this project was creating music that opens a dialogue between tradition and experimentation. We are interested in how we, as human beings, distinguish between tradition and modernity, and in the roles that technology and culture play within this relationship. Rather than reinforcing these oppositions, we wanted to explore their points of connection and reveal the creative potential that exists between them. We definitely see this collaboration as an ongoing artistic dialogue. For our next project, abandoned sites of infrastructural use from the totalitarian rule of the German Nazi regime -sites which were later also utilised by the GDR-have been chosen for recordings. These places are fascinating in that they can now be used for their acoustic qualities as instruments themselves by singing within them and ‘playing with them’, thereby alienating them from their original purpose. Of particular interest is engaging with what remains of totalitarian regimes – not necessarily sites of destruction and oppression, but sites of everyday, critical infrastructure that were an essential component in the maintenance of these systems. (Gianmarco Del Re)

The song sits second on Mang, the second EP from Guadeloupe-born sisters Laurina Moïsa and Sacha Moïsa, released 14 November 2025 on Green Piste Records. “My social power is weak,” opens the first verse, tracing a spiral of frustration, disconnection and a stutter that leaves the body behind. A rehearsed smile holds until it doesn’t, and the verse ends in tears and prayer. Then the track sharpens: a biting, hip-hop-inflected patter takes over, frontal and wound tight, as the sisters put their own mixed Guadeloupean and French heritage on the table. “My ideas come from a blood running for long, too strong,” the second verse insists, before warning off anyone still pushing: “you might upset the roots, run.” That mixed inheritance runs back to Guadeloupe, which Laurina and Sacha left as small children for mainland France, raised at home on zouk and Creole music, with a father on percussion and a mother working as a painter. A trip back to the archipelago last year reshaped the whole EP, pulling the sisters toward Creole tradition, afrobeat, soul and hip-hop inflected urban sounds sung across French, English and Creole. Percussionist Timothé Faure, who joined the sisters after they met him busking on the streets of Clermont-Ferrand, plays alongside Hadrien Mabilat‘s bass, guitar and keyboards and Nathan Pinel‘s drums; Mabilat and Mathias Chaumet mixed the track, and Yves Roussel handled mastering. items.body: 会期：2026/06/18～2026/09/21 会場：東京都写真美術館［東京都］ 公式サイト：https://topmuseum.jp/exhibition/5417/ 東京都写真美術館で映像作家・出光真子の個展「出光真子 おんなのさくひん──ある映像作家の自伝」が開催された。展示室に入ってすぐ左手に、幅90センチはあろうかというビクターの大きなブラウン管テレビが置かれている。そこには出光の代表作であり、テレビが置かれた空間を撮影することで映像内映像を生じさせる「マコ・スタイル」を用いた《主婦の一日》（1977）が映されている。本作には作家自らが出演し、ブラウン管テレビに大映しにされた出光の目が、主婦としてふるまう彼女を眺め続ける。大型テレビモニターの物量感もあいまって、日本のビデオアートの開拓者である出光の展覧会の始まりとして気持ちが昂る。 展示室は続いて、円形のカーテンブースで鑑賞地帯をゆるやかに区切りながら、70年代前半のフィルム作品から80年代のビデオ作品へとプロジェクターとテレビモニターを展開していく。とくに家庭をテーマにし、画面内にブラウン管テレビを配する作品群の上映にはテレビモニターが使われていた。 現代の平面的なディスプレイとの比較から、箱型のモニターにはオブジェとしてのかわいらしさを感じてしまうが、そこに出光真子の「マコ・スタイル」が映されるとき、テレビモニターは呪縛の歴史を露わにする装置となる。「マコ・スタイル」の背景には、家庭内にあるブラウン管テレビというメディア自体が「家に長時間いる」「主婦が見る」ものとされ、そのために主婦向けの番組が存在する一方で、テレビはまだひとりに1台という個人の所有物ではなく、一家に1台の「家庭の共有物」だった時代の翳りがある。そして展示の冒頭に置かれた巨大なテレビモニターは、彼女がそうしたテレビを買うことができた富裕家庭に育ったこと、また、それゆえに受けた家庭内抑圧の肥大さを物語るかのようでもある。 美術とフェニミニズムをめぐる観点から、これまで女性作家が「女性」という属性で一括りにされ、個々の取り組みについて評される機会が損なわれてきたことを踏まえれば、「富裕層」といった別の属性にスライドするだけの附属情報への言及は不毛に思える。しかし自らが育った環境を表象する出光作品においては、その出自の特殊さが作品の一部に組み込まれている。現時点の最新作《直近の過去》（2004）は、彼女の幼少期の家族写真と、それらと同時期に撮影された戦争の凄惨な記録を重ねたもので、そこでは出光家という一族自体が焦点化されている。 「おんなのさくひん──ある映像作家の自伝」展［筆者撮影］ 出光真子という存在が初めて公の場に出たのは、1960年12月号の『スイングジャーナル』と思われる★1。彼女はそこでアメリカやヨーロッパのジャズクラブを回ってきた「大学三年のお嬢さん」として紹介され、翌1961年には草月アートセンターにおけるジャズイベント「草月ミュージック・イン 11」にホレス・シルヴァーに国際電話をかける人物として出演する。彼女が渡米する翌1962年は、美術愛好家で出光興産の創業者でもあった出光の父が、坂倉準三に依頼した53件におよぶガソリンスタンドの建設プロジェクトが完了する年でもある★2。 美術や音楽が身近な環境で10代を過ごし、1973年に本格的に帰国するまで、渡米前から交流があったサム・フランシスと暮らしながら映像作品を手がけていく。ジュディ・シカゴらのプロジェクトを撮影した《Woman’s House》（1972）には武満徹の「ヴォーカリズムA・I」が使われるなど、美術家たちとのネットワークの中での活動が窺える。帰国後も東野芳明を通じてかわなかのぶひろと、中嶋興を通じてマイケル・ゴールドバーグと出会うなど★3、ビデオ・コミュニティが持つ協働の精神も後押しし、和田守弘や道下匡子など、多くの協力者に恵まれていく。 とくに彼女の傑作として、岸本清子とマイケル・ゴールドバーグとともに作り上げた《アニムス・パート2》（1982）を挙げたい★4。この作品には当時42〜43歳だった出光と岸本、それぞれの人生と精神がカメラに向かって開かれ、生きることと表現することが重なり合う様子、それが自然なことだとする彼女たちの佇まいが捉えられている。 本作は出光自宅のリビングルームで、自らを「地獄の使者」と称する岸本がパフォーマンスを行なう様子を1カットで撮影した映像からなる。美術家であり政治活動も行なった岸本は、権力や資本を頂点とするピラミッド型の社会構造を批判し、それを反転させた逆ピラミッド型の社会を志向する。「地獄の使者」は地へと向かう逆ピラミッドの頂点に立ち、他者のあらゆる地獄を引き受ける者で、岸本は自らがその役を担うと宣言した。彼女の思想は15分ほどの演目となり、その披露に挑む前口上から映像は始まる。 大きな窓と、その奥に広がる緑。調度品の様子など、画面に映る部屋は明らかに出光の自宅である。そのリビングの絨毯にヒールで上がり、タバコを吸い、マグカップで水分を摂取し、衣装に着替えと、どのような場であれ、自然体でふるまう岸本が捉えられている。カメラは固定だが、ときおりズームインとアウトが起こり、目の前の人物を注視するカメラマンの存在が露わになる。そしてパフォーマンスの記録映像には、出光が岸本に見出した男性性の具現化であるタイツ姿の人物の表情や身体が重ねられる。本作は出光と岸本のドキュメンタリーとしての要素に加えて、パフォーマー、カメラマン、ディレクターといった参加者との協働性が感じられるのが強い魅力である。 「おんなのさくひん──ある映像作家の自伝」展［筆者撮影］ 会場にはまた、コミュニティスペース「ホーキ星」と女性解放運動に関わった4名と制作したインスタレーション《女たち》（1977）の一部も展覧されていた★5。本作は4名のメンバーそれぞれがビデオカメラで撮影した映像と、彼女たちの撮影風景を出光が撮った映像をまとめたもの、それらの映像を全員で鑑賞しているところを撮影した6点の映像からなる。こうした構造や《主婦の一日》、《アニムス・パート2》にもあるように、出光の作品には女性の生きる姿や彼女たちが置かれた状況を率直に提示するスタイルが見られる。それはドラマ調の作品においては、フェミニストとしての理想的な姿よりも、世俗的な世界観の中で自らの弱さと対峙する女性の葛藤を描くことで現われている。 展覧会のタイトルは出光の映像作品と著書の題名から取られている。副題となった「ある映像作家の自伝」が示すように、出光の作品はある映像作家という匿名性や普遍性に、自伝という個人的な経験が合わさることで強度を放つ。ビデオカメラ黎明期の映像作家の視点と、切り分けることのできない作家と作品の関係性が照射される展覧会だった。 鑑賞日：2026/07/07（火） items.body: Review by tszirmay — This German band's debut album caught me, as well as many others by surprise, an unexpected delight. 'Six Tales of Perception' came out in 2024, and I was overjoyed to have reviewed it, egged on by the realization that Robert Kohler was a member of German prog band Inquire which I had quite relished in the past, the end result being a highly acclaimed debut rating. Still manned by two software engineers who decided to wander into musical territory and write symphonic prog can only be best described as a smart challenge to undertake and even more so, to make it successful. Keyboardist Kohler and guitarist/vocalist Dirk Krause then merged their talents as a creative force, with a unique style within a well-travelled genre. As with the debut, guest drummer Gerry Wassong handles all things percussive. "Guide to Unobtainium" (a Latinized /scientific bastardization of Unobtainable) launches the hour-long into orbit with a comfortable blast-off, Dirk's voice soothingly pleasant amid all the keyboard asteroids swooping in the space behind the microphone. The synthesizer design in particular is both bubbly and luminous. No apparent sign of electric guitars yet, an interesting detail.Quatsch! (nonsense), "Real?" immediately solves the issue as here come the buzzsaw axes, the guitars joined by the bass in unison, chopping away at my presumptuous comment. The hustling tone is electric and vigorous, without necessarily being heavy or loud, more like a feisty Mercedes race car flung along the autobahn, no brake pedal in sight, a modern rock assault that leisurely veers midway into a dreamier furrow, where the Kohler keyboards takes over and the bass helping the subtlety penetrate the arrangement. The second half of this stunning piece is addictive, but the trio reverts to the initial fury to finish off the situational irony of high expectations. Something very serious happens here. A masterful enterprise is undertaken with three tracks covering nearly 23 minutes and the fateful core of this album. "Maps Part1" takes the adventure to another twist of the story unfolding, Krause singing like a romantic crooner in softer realms, surfing on a sea of synthesized pleasure, a throttling axe splurge to keep the agony going. There will be a "Maps Part 2" , once the fifteen-mile excursion into an epic 10-minute trek in the desert, searching for the mystical "Valley of the Deep". The Oriental-tinge is unmistakable, the growling organ caravan showing no remorse in the mirage-laden imagery, the sun suddenly broiling, the tea kettle boiling and the Seraglio blowing up a sandstorm on the endless horizon. This is one hell of a cinematographic highlight, expertly woven like the finest silk, close one's eyes and flutter into fantasy land of sonic wonder. There's the rub, it may have sounded like crossover before but now, its outright symphonic. The second Maps chapter keeps the mood glowing, cleverly incorporating the two previous sections, welded together by a titanic mellotron torrent that should blow your tropical helmets into the furthest oasis (if there is one anywhere close). The lyrics on the intoxicating chorus encompass the spirit perfectly 'Let's forget the world we live in, let's embrace the hope we feel' and 'Lets accept the deal and give in. Let's pretend the map is real'. Sign of times, wot? One hell of an epic this, as the Brits say 'No over-egg the pudding here'. The bar is set very high in the sky, but "Sadness" keeps the atmosphere alight with a drop-dead perfect segue, a distressed melodic embrace that exudes so much passion and feeling, it's hard not to gulp in admiration. Yearning for some kind of eventual salvation, the hushed Krause voice only adding enigma to the endless ache, the instrumental melodicism and attention to detail simply off the charts and compelling, 'and you are left with the words that only you can hear'. Shifting to "Before My Eyes", the acoustic guitars and melancholic style coming straight out classic Strawbs pantheon, liquid synthesizer and flowing organ adornments, all within a pastoral, countrified setting, I could not help feeling relief from all the previous symphonic overload having pounded me into willing submission. This is utter mellotron panacea and absolutely gorgeous. "Exit Right" as the title may imply, restores a more reflective sombreness, the lyrics particularly indicative of the overtly complexity we all seem to drown in, stressed by endless beeps, flickers and dross. The two steps forward, three steps back syndrome. The synths seem to cry, the bass grumbling along and the guitars bellowing in raging afterthought. "But the code has a bug in its logic', well two software engineers should know. The up-front and bellicose bass is simply wonderful on "Scene of A Crime", a suspenseful foray into detective work, lest we forget that the who and mostly the why come much later, when and where always the first to be determined. We often get that wrong as well, as lying is the oldest subterfuge. The arrangement favours all kinds of spooky and dramatic sounds, as if created with a wink to Gowan's Criminal Mind classic or Falco's Jenny (if you are unaware, look them up !), this case owns the same 'guilty as charged' vibe. The extended axe solo is, excuse the pun?killer! "Dreamers" is the welcome finale, as it suggest a positive outcome, after all the twists and turns on the roller coaster of life, we get to rest, and hopefully dream, a merciful reprieve from all the stress daily life can provide at will, seemingly. Imperfect silence, perhaps, but still peace. I gave very high marks to the debut and deservedly so. I never thought this could be even better. Its amazing. 5 Handbooks to nothing

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Drawing on extensive experience in the Swedish jazz scene as they ventured into rock, Hawk on Flight utilized the full range of the quartet's capabilities; "Beyond My Rocks" begins with echoes of Herbie Hancock's Head Hunters, Likewise, Ulf Wakenius's virtuosity on the jazz guitar traversed the realm of rock, tracing a fine melodic line in between.Jag Tanker displays its own rhythmic style within the genre's conventions, where keyboards and synthesizers provide a bed for the bass and guitar to rest upon, while Fat Freddy's Cat blends jazz-rock with disco rhythms, without losing a funk orientation, alongside those drawn-out grooves.Every guitar lick on Landscapes foreshadows future productions, showing a certain inclination toward various forms of fusion. Here, the piano and drums draw upon the classic jazz tradition, while the bass charts its own course with a more modern, solitary approach, a welcome and healthy counterpoint."Hawk on Flight" presents a mid-tempo track featuring synthesizer embellishments, with an almost psychedelic, hypnotic, and atmospheric quality, that enrich the underlying rhythmic foundation. Matz Nilsson's bass stands out for its energetic, driving character, interacting with H�kon Graf's keyboards; Graf fuses Weather Report influences with a funk sensibility to shape the closing track, "In Time."Even while still searching for their sound, they discovered pure fusion within the very process of that search, following the arrow toward their own path.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The fact that Frode Thingn�s's quintet included two members of Popol Ace, Thor Andreassen on drums and Pete Knutsen on guitar, meant the group benefited from the shift toward a fusion-style groove; combined with the timbre of Frode's trombone, a saxophonist, and two additional drummers, the music certainly didn't lack rhythm.Tracks ranging from "Soapy Crow" to "After Hours" are reminiscent of the solo work of Billy Cobham, who often incorporated horns into his funk-infused rhythms. On Samba Loco, he obviously flirts with Latin rhythms, but through the sophisticated lens of Latin jazz, featuring trombone solos in the style of Ray Anderson or Robin Eubanks and delightful flute work play by Henryk Lysiak and reminiscent of Dave Valentin, all backed by a funk-infused band, until "Abraxas" introduces more guitar fusion, with the trombone taking a near-lead role in a rock-oriented style.The Rhodes is in play, and while it may not shatter genre boundaries, sometimes the point is simply to enjoy something well-crafted; at times, there are calm passages, hence the title, that add almost cinematic nuances, evoking the kind of poetry characteristic of that era.As it is a trombonist's album, it is rich in the use of chromatics, particularly in the interplay between the saxophone and the Moog synthesizers. Night Sounds concludes with the title track, a danceable jazz-rock piece featuring plenty of funk, rhythm changes, and syncopation, while also offering a variety of textures to appreciate.Above all, it is evident that he was a composer and conductor first and an instrumentalist second, as the arrangements are defined down to the smallest detail, a meticulousness appreciated by a certain segment of the genre.

The band uses a minimalist approach with plenty of emotion in the music. Noinstrument overshadows another. The band doesn't use many notes but delivers the perfect sound andmelody that keeps you on the edge from the first note to the last. From the first song, the vocalsand the guitar remind me of the music of Ennio Morricone. Then it goes into a Tubular Bells kind ofpassage, but with an added spacey touch. Some breathtaking piano and synths continue to carry themelody. The album has to be listened to in one take, like one great song.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Paolo Pagliari offers melodic, atmospheric sounds built upon a classic prog foundation. Echoes of Genesis, Pink Floyd, Camel, Marillion, and APP or BJH combine to create elegant progressive rock with cinematic arrangements."So Begins" opens with schoolyard shouts and a cinematic-symphonic prog build-up?evoking a "Close Encounters" atmosphere as memories come flooding back. A martial snare drum drives the track?a musical offspring of Supertramp, Pink Floyd, and Camel?accompanied by a parade of guitars. "Stars in Your Eyes" begins with a Floydian feel; the organ adds melodic depth while the guitar rides a Gilmour-esque wave. Paolo's vocals?backed by Doryan and Silvia?deliver a sugary, radio-friendly prog tune (reminiscent of Alan Parsons) that packs a killer riff. It culminates in a soaring, extended guitar solo that brings Big Big Train to mind. "Father's Words" is a gentle track, redolent of Barclay James Harvest, recounting a slice of life from a lovingly nurtured childhood. It features a pastoral, Genesis-style air?complete with flute, Mellotron, and a commanding piano?while the guitar solo evokes the legends of the genre. Guest musician Luca works his magic, blending influences from the Beatles, New Wave, Roxy Music, and Marillion to create an explosive sound that is a pure delight for the ears; simple yet beautiful, it leads into the sound of rain that introduces "Watching Through the Window on a Melancholic Rainy Day." This track features a delicate arpeggio intermezzo?reminiscent of Dire Straits?evoking a pastoral mood against the backdrop of a rain-streaked window. The flute calls to mind the melancholic soundscapes of Genesis as the rain falls."Hold On!" takes us back in time with its quintessential 70s sound?Beatles-esque vocals paired with organ and folk flute. A nostalgic Hammond organ solo cuts through the air, satisfying the prog fan's craving for something new. "Lune de Mer" follows?a cinematic, maritime moment where the flute seems to walk upon the waves, and where "Wilson Junior" candidly asks for the song's title. "In the Shelter of Your Eyes" has a Parsons-esque feel to the melody and a Floydian touch in the fluid guitar work. It is a meltingly sweet tune that stirs the senses with its cool, jazzy atmosphere and a guitar solo that drifts along, leading into the finale?"Camel Escape"?which launches into an *Arabian Nights* vibe, a lunar journey with a camel as the backdrop. It is a clear homage to that forgotten dinosaur of a band, with its lush melodies and fluid, airy guitar work reminiscent of Gilmour during the melting instrumental sections."Memory Box" is solemn and languid, reflecting on life's experiences, the ticking of the clock, and memories. Faint vocal traces and a flute weave over crystalline arpeggios?or vice versa. A melancholic guitar extends the nostalgic mood, building into a dreamlike swell that segues into "Light in the Night"; the latter begins with vocals, with "Memory" serving as its intro. The warm backing vocals from Luca and Irene and the sweet melody?accentuated by the Hammond organ?show a well-honed sound. The nod to the Alan Parsons Project continues: grandiose and pompous, much like the Barclay James Harvest of yesteryear, complete with a vintage-style outro.A unique style of symphonic prog rock featuring three instrumentals; it flirts with neo-prog, inviting the listener into a realm of musical reverie and introspection. (4.25)

items.body: Review by alainPP — LUNATIC SOUL, Mariusz DUDA and his desire to compose alone, a best-combination album following the saga of his seventh album, "Through Shaded Woods," released in 2020. Between life and death."Realm of the Weeping Willows," the only unreleased track, comes from the "Through Shaded Woods" recording sessions. A staccato ambient rhythm in four parts, with the aggression of the bass, the captivating organ, the mantra-like drums?in short, a sound that could easily be found on RIVERSIDE. An air from the austere Polish regions with the tambourine and acoustic guitar, an invitation to travel beyond the steppes, the flute completing the spell. The vocals fade into the distance, but RIVERSIDE is still present, the grief not yet fully processed; crescendoing prog rock sets its mid-cycle break.A Marillion-esque folk melancholy, almost angelic in the air?those already familiar with the genre will surely recognize it. This ambient passage plunges into darkness, contemplation, a shadowy, ethereal journey, with hylophobia as a backdrop. The finale, with its vibrant strings and Mariusz's choir, melts away, injecting mystery and solemnity into the long, repetitive final sound."Hylophobia," known for its sharp riff from the 2020 bonus album, still carries that unsettling feeling linked to forests. A punchy, explosive rock track with a sharp bass line; midway through, the religious, mantra-like, folk-liturgical choir appears, unchanged from the original. "Vyraj," with bass and organ, instruments of the era, is undoubtedly a nod to Dead Can Dance. A grumpy, raging folk-dance rock track; A track flirting with the great Mike Oldfield in a heavy metal version, inviting a hypnotic musical addiction. An entry into Mariusz's singular universe, his bewitching mythical paradise, beyond the Milky Way. An abrasive, percussive tempo seems to emerge from a distant past, the vocals whispered, the organ bouncing, and the bass captivating."Transition II" remixed and shorter for its LP version. Seven parts featuring an archaic flute, Mariusz narrating a story as if wandering, much like on Riverside. A slow and progressive start, linear and tribal, with an ethereal piano reminiscent of Simple Minds. Three minutes of intro before the techno bass, metallic percussion, and stereo vocals explain the encounter with the Ferryman for the transition. A pounding, contemplative experience, perhaps challenging for some, this track could easily be played in a nightclub deep in the forest, on the banks of a river like the Styx. The break from the folk atmosphere reminiscent of Oldfield, a xylophone and guitar surfing in its own world; cinematic sounds on Inspector Gadget, the music of Reich, Richter, sparkling, emerging from the melancholy inhabiting Mariusz; a way of compensating for his break with Riverside.A panting, a race to distance himself from his band, and the atmosphere shifts to a cinematic soundtrack evoking The Big Blue, airy, crystalline, on Apsaras. The light is definitely there, bringing gaiety to his notes; a little reminder of "Transition 1," about the birth of his son. The guitar suddenly leans towards Tangerine Dream before cutting to this solemn piano, ambient Pink Floyd, distant new age, stereo, recalling the album "Impressions" and snippets of Ange and Barclay James Harvest. This music is remarkable, skillfully balancing nostalgia, emotion, and sensitivity, allowing us to transcend the ending of RIVERSIDE. The final ambient, cinematic outro, reminiscent of TANGERINE DREAM, is reminiscent of Tangram and Force Majeure.LUNATIC SOUL, a musical chrysalis, metamorphoses into ambient, electronic music. An atmospheric, progressive folk sound that feels fresh and hopeful. A remix album with a beautiful unreleased track feels a bit underwhelming. (3.5)

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — I feel like I've just come out of a shopping mall, but instead of bags and shoe boxes, I'm stuffing a mountain of musical concepts and ideas into my trunk. This is my first handshake with this band, and I'm glad I'm starting my listening experience with Pure Reason Revolution's debut album "The Dark Third". This album is a really unique blending of influences. In the most general terms, it feels like indie rock, but one that ventures into the epic. Gosh, there's so much to distill here: I hear Disney on weed. I hear psychedelia. I hear progressive rock. I hear Beach Boys-style pop. I hear electronica. I hear Zeppelin. I hear Steven Wilson/ Porcupine Tree...I guess you could say this album, and maybe this band, is all about layers: heavy antique curtains, or a chiffon-layered cake.Listening to this record has brought something important to mind: you really need to listen to a band's album from start to finish. Everybody loves a good song, but it's through the full body of their work that you really start to get to know a band. You start to get a sense of their strengths as musicians, but also who they are as a creative unit?their instincts, their ideas, their chemistry. You get to hear how they move from one idea to another, how they build an album, and ultimately, you get a taste of the full wingspan of a band's psyche.This point really hit home after my first listen to The Dark Third. For example, the album finishes with an amazingly subtle musical farewell?a phrase that you can only really appreciate if you've journeyed with the band from the first song to the last. It's like skipping ahead and reading the final page of a book. You can know how it ends, but you don't have the context. You need to experience the whole journey?all the twists and turns, all the contours, to really understand where that ending takes you. And to me, that's the essence, and the fun of it. That's why I'm here, frankly, telling you all this!The core lineup is Jon Courtney on vocals/guitar/keyboards, Chlo� Alper on vocals/bass, Jamie Willcox on vocals/guitar, Jim Dobson on keyboards/guitar/bass/violin/vocals and Andrew Courtney on drums.Instrumentally, there's a lot of clean electric guitar, both strummed and picked, as well as some bottle-neck slide. That's not to say the doors don't get completely blown off the barn in bursts of classic-rock riffing and inspired sections throughout this very energetic album. There's also a good smattering of violin, both clean and distorted, along with some very full-sounding string ensemble arrangements.There are plenty of atmospheric passages too, featuring synths and echoing guitars, and piano gets its share of the spotlight. The production is dynamic and creative, handled by Paul Northfield, whose credits include Dream Theater, Rush, and Porcupine Tree. The drums are often very textural and treated or combined with electronic beats, with some interesting processing and effects applied at the mixing desk. There's some rainy and wet sounding cymbal accents from the drums.Compositionally, there are zero weak tracks or sections. The structure is often tumbling and unpredictable with ideas constantly shifting, colliding, and reconfiguring.The vocals are a highlight, often heavily layered, with contrasting vocal lines making for a rich, textured sound. Of course, the two main singers, male and female, work exceptionally well together, complementing each other nicely.Lyrically, The Dark Third is a pretty surreal album. It gets into the subconscious, dreams, sleep, and that blurry line between what's real and what's happening in your head. There's literary and philosophical influence, but the lyrics do feel like a stream of consciousness. Even the title refers to that 'dark third' of our lives?the time we spend asleep and dreaming.So really, this is a satisfying, fairly dense and rich, high calorie album. I really enjoy the time I spend with it. It's a 4.5 out of 5 dog bones (or stars on progarchives) because it does everything an album is supposed to do, and when I get to the finish I usually want to start it all over again. The songs flow into each other and it has no weak or filler tracks. It's engaging and interesting at every turn, decked out with amazing vocal layers throughout.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — "You can't handle the truth" was a great line in a great movie, but there's something in that idea that applies to all of us. We like to imagine we're the exception, that we're ready to face whatever truth comes our way.Chasm feels like a pretty good test of that assumption.I find Chasm, by The Tea Club, to be a deep album, as deep as the title implies?but it isn't a dangerous place to go. Quite the opposite. I loved it from the get-go. It's funny how, historically speaking, artists have sometimes been deemed dangerous by overzealous governments and dictatorships. Maybe it's because art can be so individual and unique, and therefore inherently threatening to any force that demands conformity and uniformity. Art has a way of saying, I see the world differently.And it's not easy being an artist. Not that an artist necessarily has to suffer in order to create good work, but they often have to work damn hard to bring that work into the world. It's a little like giving birth to something that then needs to be cared for and nurtured until it can stand on its own two feet?and protected along the way from all the harsh elements that might keep it from surviving.That's one reason the first thing that amazed me about Chasm was how original The Tea Club sound. There are recognizable influences here, of course, but the combination feels distinctly their own. And beneath that originality is an enormous amount of raw energy and forward drive, coupled with these deeper currents of yearning, for connection, for meaning, perhaps even for wholeness.Chasm is not overly polished, and clearly isn't aiming to please the music machines so much as reach for something beyond and somewhere else. I feel like the more I dig into this album, the more it will reveal itself. It's heartfelt, often bursting with honest energy and emotion, chasing ideas but also taking the time to pause and take stock.The songwriting is strong and bold. The Tea Club's sound is reminiscent of grunge and '80s King Crimson/Adrian Belew, with hints of a youthful Sting and The Police. There's also a hint of Metric with a male vocalist. There are no long epics here?just short ones. There's lots of bending and building going on here, with a touch of madness. If this album got sucked into an AI song-creation algorithm, it would probably become confused and label the whole thing a corrupted file. There are brief moments when Chasm becomes almost anti-melodic, but purposefully so, I suspect?creating contrast with the melodies that emerge around them.You can hear this particularly well on "Vineyard". The Tea Club mostly recorded this album as a band playing live off the floor, all analog, rather than surgically piecing performances together at different times and in different places. That sense of musicians interacting in real time comes through. The drums act as the glue, while the chorus winds like a river through unexpected and beautiful chords. It sounds less like a collection of individually constructed parts and more like a proper band listening to and responding to each other in the moment.If I were a cigar-smoking record exec, I'd be yelling, "I don't hear any hits!" And this is a good thing. Long live the anti-hits emerging from the antimatter universe. There is one curiously arresting track- 'The Lunar Eclipse', a pretty and sweet piano based song that the band reports to having struggled with in the recording phase and in the album track sequencing phase. Putting it last seems the perfect cap or cherry on the top to this adventurous album, and is one of my favourite tracks along with the album opener and 'Vineyard'. So, this bold album is not for the timid traveller. It's for the vigorous and strong prog-at-heart music appreciator?the kind of listener willing to dig in and discover what's hiding in the chasm. I give it a 4.5 out of 5 dog bones (or 4/5 stars on progarchives)
