items.body: With “Realities”, Jan Dewulf does something more interesting than simply broaden Mildreda‘s sound. He removes one of the most recognisable elements of “Blue-Devilled” altogether: there is not a single sacred sample on the new album. The quasi-liturgical weight of its predecessor gives way to colder electronics, sharper industrial abrasion and passages that move considerably closer to noise. At the same time, the writing becomes more exposed, allowing tenderness, ageing, regret, loneliness and vulnerability into Mildreda without translating any of them into softness. Scheduled for release on August 28 through Dependent Records, “Realities” is an 18-track double album, also issued as a limited 2CD artbook with 48 pages designed by Henk Willems. Recurring “Reality Checks” run through its structure; Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada appears on “Rückwärts”, while Suicide Commando‘s Johan Van Roy joins “Virtual Goddess”. Where “Blue-Devilled” worked explicitly with Sartre, “Realities” turns towards Camus and Sisyphus: falling, rebuilding and the uncomfortable recognition that a life does not unfold inside one stable reality, but through successive versions of it. In this conversation, that idea moves far beyond philosophy as an intellectual reference. Dewulf talks about reaching middle age and the lives no longer available to us, why the “Reality Checks” function like the seams in kintsugi, social media complicity, the strange persistence of gods after belief disappears, and why increased vulnerability pushed Mildreda towards more violent sound rather than away from it. The result is also a remarkably precise account of an artist who says he is no longer searching for Mildreda’s identity; he is now interested in finding out how far that identity can be stretched before it stops being Mildreda. Realities by Mildreda Mildreda interview Karo: Jan, when we first spoke in 2021, you told me that maturity had finally allowed you to “come home” with Mildreda. I have followed the project ever since, through “I Was Never Really There”, “Blue-Devilled”, the concerts and now “Realities”, and this record gives me almost the opposite impression: you sound secure enough in Mildreda to start dismantling parts of the language you had established. How much did making “Realities” require you to question your own idea of what Mildreda is supposed to sound like? Jan: You could argue that making music, playing in a band, writing lyrics and creating a story around it will always be a journey of exploration. But the nature of that journey has definitely changed. I’m no longer searching for Mildreda’s identity, and by now I feel I’ve figured out the DNA of the project as well. That foundation is there, and it’s solid. And precisely because of that, I can now embark on more adventurous quests: exploring the boundaries of the Mildreda sound, allowing for a broader emotional range, and seeing how far I can stretch things without losing what makes Mildreda what it is. I think that’s something you can clearly hear on “Realities”. Karo: When you sent me the album, you described it as your most emotional work and said there were “more colours in the music than ever”. Having heard it, I think the interesting thing is that those colours are certainly not all softer ones. There is industrial abrasion, noise, harsher vocals, but also enormous electronic detail, space and moments of delicacy. When you speak about colour in music, what exactly does that mean to you? Is it timbre, emotional range, dynamics, harmonic language, or the freedom to allow contradictory emotional states to exist within the same musical vocabulary? Jan: When I said it was my most emotional album, I also, and perhaps primarily, meant that on a lyrical level. I allowed myself to explore themes and emotions that are rather unusual within a genre like dark electro. I deliberately moved beyond the genre’s more traditional themes of pain, anger and darkness, making room for vulnerability and tenderness instead. That vulnerability sometimes finds its way into the music as well, in quieter, more emotional and delicate passages that are relatively new territory for Mildreda. But at the same time, I really pushed the boundaries in the opposite direction too, exploring noisier, harsher and more abrasive territory than before. So in that sense, those additional colours aren’t necessarily softer ones. It’s more about widening the entire emotional and sonic spectrum of what Mildreda can be. Karo: The distance from “Blue-Devilled” is wide. That album had an almost architectural darkness, with quasi-sacral space, ritual weight and gothic grandeur, whereas “Realities” feels more corporeal, metallic and exposed. The church-like atmosphere has largely disappeared even though the philosophical conflict has not. Did the change in subject matter make that previous sonic language inappropriate, or had you simply reached the point where you no longer needed those symbols to create darkness? Jan: Especially in Mildreda’s early days in the 1990s, that sacred element was an important part of the sound. I was heavily influenced by bands like Will, early Delerium and In Slaughter Natives, who incorporated bombastic samples of sacred chants into their dark electronic compositions. That whole wave of inspiration came back in full force while making “Blue-Devilled”, so much so that the album is packed with grandiose, sacral samples. One fan joked that if he took a shot of jenever every time he heard a monk singing on “Blue-Devilled”, he’d be completely drunk by the end of the album. He had a point: we may have overdone it a little. So with “Realities”, it was a very conscious decision not to use a single sacred sample anywhere on the album. This time, I wanted the darkness to come from a colder, more purely electronic sound. Karo: “Blue-Devilled” entered into dialogue with Sartre, particularly his idea of hell in relation to the gaze and judgement of other people. “Realities” moves towards Camus, which changes the philosophical problem considerably: from the self confronted by another consciousness towards the collision between our need for meaning and a world that does not promise to provide it. Why did Camus become relevant to you now, and was that movement philosophical first or biographical first? Jan: At its heart, “Realities” is about falling down and finding the strength to get back up again. Throughout our lives, we keep having to rediscover and rebuild ourselves after setbacks, whether they are small or life-changing. And we have to do all of that within the brief interlude we are granted in this universe: our finite lives. That is where Camus entered the picture. In many ways, “Realities” became a confrontation with the absurd. Echoing Camus and his comparison of the human condition to the fate of Sisyphus, the album revolves around that endless cycle of falling and rising, breaking and rebuilding, and forcing ourselves to create new versions of reality. We search for meaning even though the universe offers us no guarantee that there is any to be found. And yet we keep moving. That is also exactly what the title “Realities” refers to. We don’t live in one single, fixed reality, but in a succession of realities. With every setback, every decision and every new beginning, we become a slightly different version of ourselves and inhabit a slightly different world. Visually, that journey is beautifully reflected in Henk Willems’ artwork, where nature slowly reclaims what was once broken. Moss spreads across abandoned ruins, while new growth gradually softens the scars of destruction. To me, it became a powerful metaphor for the album itself: not simply a story of collapse, but of renewal. Not of defeat, but of return. Karo: Camus famously concludes “The Myth of Sisyphus” with “One must imagine Sisyphus happy”, but your Sisyphus in “End of the Line” carries something rather more specific: biography. “Forty-five, fifty-five / This is the time of your life”, followed by those “thousand lives you never led”, introduces age, memory and unrealised possibility into the cycle. Returning to the beginning at fifty cannot mean returning to the same beginning as at twenty because the person pushing the rock has accumulated knowledge, losses and consequences. Does your Sisyphus still arrive at something resembling Camus’s freedom through lucidity, or are you questioning whether accepting the absurd is enough once time itself has become part of the burden? Jan: The initial spark was actually something very personal. Not that long ago, when I turned 45, someone told me, “You’re about to enter the ten best years of your life.” Whether that’s true or not is impossible to say, of course, but there was something strangely powerful about that thought. It almost felt like an obligation to make those years count. That naturally led me back to questions that have always fascinated me: the fact that life is finite, that our time is limited, and that with age comes an increasing awareness of all the lives we could have lived but didn’t. At twenty, there still seems to be an almost infinite number of possible futures ahead of you. Later in life, some of those possibilities have inevitably disappeared. Choices have been made, things have been lost, and time itself becomes part of the weight you carry. That is where Camus and Sisyphus became particularly relevant to “End of the Line”. Sisyphus keeps pushing his boulder despite knowing that it will inevitably roll back down. To me, that endless cycle of falling, getting back up and starting again is a very powerful metaphor for life. We all have our own rock to push uphill, and somehow we keep going. So can Sisyphus still be happy while carrying that rock up the mountain again and again? I think, with Camus, that he can. Despite our mortality and the intrinsic meaninglessness of existence, we still have the freedom to create our own stories, to find joy and to give meaning to the limited time we have. Perhaps age doesn’t contradict Camus’s idea of freedom at all; it simply makes it more urgent. We’d better start pushing, living and creating meaning now, because at some point, the time really does run out. Karo: Musically, I hear more industrial language on “Realities” than on any previous Mildreda album, sometimes moving into very raw, almost noise-like territory. “Rückwärts” is particularly severe and fragmented, but that hardness runs through much of the record in the percussion, distortion, chopped structures and increasingly sharp vocal attack. What led you towards these harsher materials? Did you consciously pursue abrasion as part of the production language, and were there moments when you had to resist making a sound cleaner because its discomfort was exactly what the song required? Jan: That direction actually emerged quite naturally. But it is true that, with this album, I consciously wanted the music to be less immediately digestible than on the previous record. Musically, “Realities” has far more sharp edges, rough textures and moments of genuine abrasion. Perhaps I had been a little too cautious before, whereas this time I allowed myself to go all the way. There is a certain duality at the heart of the album in that respect: very harsh, abrasive music intertwined with vulnerability in the lyrics and themes. That contrast has always fascinated me. Nine Inch Nails taught me that industrial music can be layered with vulnerability without losing any of its power or aggression. If anything, the two can reinforce each other. Karo: At the same time, reducing “Realities” to its aggression would completely misrepresent it because this is also an extraordinarily elaborate electronic record. Across the album, sounds accumulate, separate, change depth and move around one another; dense structures can suddenly open and allow a small sample, voice or electronic detail to occupy an enormous amount of psychological space. How differently were you thinking about density, depth and layering this time, and how do you know when complexity is intensifying an emotion rather than beginning to hide it? Jan: First of all, thank you for describing our music so beautifully. I’m genuinely happy that I was able to take you along on that musical journey in that way. For me, every track is a new search for the right sound and the right balance. And I love that process. I find it incredibly rewarding to spend hours in the studio working with synths and samples, tweaking sounds and layers until they evoke exactly the feeling I’m looking for. There’s something wonderful about that moment when, after endless tweaking, the pieces of the puzzle suddenly fall into place. This time, there simply seemed to be more puzzle pieces than ever, all demanding their own space. That’s one of the reasons why “Realities” ultimately needed to become a double album. I secretly hope that listeners will surrender to that journey from beginning to end: eighteen tracks moving through very different moods, textures and sonic landscapes. For me, the complexity only works when all those layers ultimately serve that journey and the emotion behind it. Karo: The “Reality Checks” are one of the strongest compositional ideas on the album. I do not hear them as conventional interludes because they do not merely separate the larger songs or give us recovery time. They make the whole record feel interwoven, almost braided: the substantial compositions form one strand, these smaller pieces enter between them, and gradually the relationship between the two becomes part of the album’s architecture. When did you realise that “Realities” needed this structure, and what makes an idea a “Reality Check” rather than something that develops into a full Mildreda song? Jan: The idea of using interludes was there from the very beginning. I wanted something that would weave the individual songs together and make the album feel like one continuous journey rather than simply a collection of tracks. Albums like “Entities” by Project Pitchfork and “Galleries of Pain” by Placebo Effect were important references in that respect. Gradually, those interludes developed a character of their own and became the “Reality Checks”. I started to see them almost as the golden seams in kintsugi: they sit between the larger pieces, but rather than simply separating them, they bind the fractured parts into a new whole. Some echo or distort elements from the songs around them, some contain vocals, while others became little sonic adventures of their own. And perhaps that is what distinguishes a “Reality Check” from a full Mildreda song. It doesn’t need to arrive anywhere or tell a complete story. It can remain fragmentary: suggest something, disturb the balance for a moment and then disappear. Its incompleteness is part of its purpose. Karo: Their placement also gives the album something almost physiological, like a heartbeat. Pressure accumulates, then comes a caesura, a moment of recalibration, and movement resumes. Yet the “Reality Checks” are not predictable moments of relief; sometimes they open the music and allow it to breathe, while elsewhere they make the footing even less secure. In ordinary life, a reality check is exactly such a moment: the narrative we have been living inside is interrupted and we are forced to take stock of where we actually stand. Afterwards the external circumstances may be identical, but our perception of them has changed. Is that also what these pieces are doing, repeatedly altering the position from which we perceive the music around them, and perhaps offering another way of understanding the plural title “Realities”? Jan: Yes, very much so. I like your description of them as moments of recalibration, because that is exactly how I see a reality check in life as well. Something happens that briefly disrupts the story you have been telling yourself. The world may still be exactly the same afterwards, but your position within it has shifted. That connects directly to the central idea of “Realities”. We fall, we rise, we rebuild ourselves, and each time we do, we are forced into a slightly different version of reality. There is no single fixed perspective from which we experience our lives. Our perception constantly changes through loss, experience, decisions and new beginnings. “Reality Checks” translate that idea into the architecture of the album. They interrupt the flow and slightly reposition the listener before the next piece begins. And importantly, as you point out, they are not always moments of relief. Sometimes a reality check brings clarity; sometimes it only makes things more confusing. But either way, something has shifted. You continue the journey from a different position than before. And yes, in that sense they are very closely connected to the plural in “Realities”: there is never just one reality to return to. Karo: You told me that the material grew into a double album, yet for you it still tells one story. That is a difficult structural problem: eighteen pieces, radically different degrees of intensity and a very broad electronic vocabulary could easily become abundance without coherence. At what point did you understand that you were not making two albums, or an album with supplementary pieces? What makes “Realities” one work for you: narrative, emotional continuity, musical recurrence, or something that only exists through the sequence itself? Jan: There was also a very practical starting point. New albums on Dependent are nowadays released as beautiful, exclusive hardcover artbooks with two CDs. I’m a big fan of that format, but I’m not necessarily a big fan of the idea that the second disc automatically has to become a collection of bonus material. I didn’t feel like inviting a dozen remixers for this one. This had to remain my story. So in a way, I was quite happy to discover that I simply had too much to say for a single CD. There were so many musical ideas, moods and little sonic adventures that all felt integral to the same universe. Cutting them down just to fit the conventional length of an album would have felt more artificial than allowing the record to expand. And there was a reassuring precedent, of course. Nine Inch Nails showed with “The Fragile” that a double album can be an extraordinary work in its own right rather than an album plus an appendix. That record gave me confidence that abundance doesn’t necessarily have to come at the expense of coherence. For me, “Realities” is ultimately one big story. Despite the range of sounds, moods and emotions, everything belongs to the same conceptual journey: falling, rebuilding, shifting perspective and entering another reality. The “Reality Checks” help bind that journey together, but ultimately I think the coherence exists in the sequence itself. I hope the listener experiences those eighteen pieces not as separate destinations, but as chapters in one long journey through constantly changing emotional and sonic landscapes. Karo: In our first interview you described songwriting as a way of exorcising your demons. “Realities”, however, seems less protected by symbolic architecture than some of the earlier material. “Damage Done”, “Clair-Obscur” and “End of the Line” allow loneliness, emotional asymmetry, ageing, regret and exhaustion to remain recognisably human rather than disguising them completely as theology or elaborate metaphor. Has becoming more personal also changed your relationship with abstraction? At what point does transforming an experience protect the song, and at what point does it protect the writer too much? Jan: That is something that happened quite naturally and evolved over time. Initially, Your Life On Hold was the project where I allowed myself to reveal more of my soul and dig deeper into personal emotions, while Mildreda was primarily the place where I wanted to be loud, confrontational and channel aggression. But gradually, while writing new material, I found myself digging deeper with Mildreda as well. I started allowing a much broader emotional range into the project and became less dependent on abstraction or metaphor to express what I wanted to say. I think that also has a lot to do with becoming more confident as a songwriter. I no longer feel the need to hide behind anything. If there is something I want to say, I can say it openly and without disguise. And what changed with “Realities” is that I discovered I can do that within Mildreda too, without compromising what Mildreda is. Karo: You mentioned Nine Inch Nails to me while explaining the direction of this record, particularly the possibility of allowing vulnerability and emotional depth to coexist with intensity and noise. On “Realities”, vulnerability rarely means making the music gentler; quite often exposure seems to make it more violent. Did that become a compositional principle in itself, that tenderness, humiliation, rage, longing and industrial aggression do not need separate musical languages because they can actually originate from the same emotional state? Jan: What is vulnerable, fragile and delicate is also more susceptible to pain, and I think you can hear that throughout the album. There is a lot of sadness, underlying pain and unanswered longing on “Realities”. Those emotions don’t necessarily ask for gentle music. Sometimes vulnerability can be extremely violent precisely because there is so little protection around it. The best way for me to translate that duality into music was therefore sometimes to work with very dissonant, abrasive and explosive sounds. Tenderness and aggression don’t have to be opposites; they can grow out of exactly the same emotional state. That constant interplay between light and shadow runs through the entire album, I think. The fragile moments make the harsh ones more painful, and the harshness in turn makes the vulnerability feel even more exposed. Karo: The collaborators introduce another interesting contradiction. In 2023 you told me that with “Blue-Devilled” you deliberately wanted to undertake the creative process yourself, partly because after previous collaborations you needed to demonstrate that you could stand alone artistically. “Realities”, which you consider much more personal, opens the door again: Constantin Warter of Calva Y Nada enters “Rückwärts”, while Johan Van Roy of Suicide Commando appears on “Virtual Goddess”. Why did the more personal album become the right place for other voices again, and how much of their own identity do you want a guest to bring into a Mildreda song? Jan: That’s true: on “Blue-Devilled” I deliberately avoided collaborations for exactly the reason you mention. But that was an artistic decision rather than something dictated by the subject matter. I needed to prove to myself that I could carry an entire Mildreda album on my own. Once I had done that, there was no reason to keep that door closed. This time I wanted other voices on the record, and I’m incredibly happy with the people I managed to bring in. The collaboration with Calva Y Nada was actually a blessing on a very practical level as well. “Rückwärts” was one of the first songs I wrote for the album, but after living with the demo for a while, I realised I was completely stuck. I loved the track, but I simply couldn’t imagine my own voice doing it justice. Constantin has such a unique and unmistakable voice that once I started fantasising about someone else singing it, I simply couldn’t hear anyone but him. Through mutual friends we got in touch, eventually met in person, and to my delight he connected with the idea. For me, it was a genuine full-circle moment. Calva Y Nada was one of the bands that defined my teenage years, so hearing Constantin’s voice on a Mildreda record still feels both surreal and deeply meaningful. Johan Van Roy represents something very similar to me. Together with Dirk Ivens, he helped shape what dark electro sounded like in Belgium. With “Realities”, I deliberately wanted to reconnect with that cold, uncompromising Belgian industrial DNA, and “Virtual Goddess” immediately felt like the perfect track for Johan. He brought exactly the intensity and attitude I had hoped for. And I think that also answers the question of how much of themselves I want guests to bring. I don’t invite someone simply to perform a part that could just as easily have been sung by me. I want their identity to become part of the song. Constantin and Johan are unmistakably themselves on these tracks, while somehow still sounding completely at home within Mildreda. Having them both on “Realities” is a real privilege. They are far more than guest vocalists to me: they are two artists whose music helped shape my own musical identity long before Mildreda even existed. Karo: The remixes take that question of identity even further. Das Ich and Steril reconstruct “End of the Line”, while Flesh Field rework “Virtual Goddess”, and around a record called “Realities” the very act of remixing becomes conceptually appropriate: the same composition receives another body, another emphasis and another emotional temperature while remaining recognisable. Did any of those versions make you discover something in your own original that you had not consciously put there? More fundamentally, where does the identity of a song reside if rhythm, texture, atmosphere and structure can change so dramatically while we still perceive it as the same work? Jan: I have a bit of a love-hate relationship with remixes. I love them when they have a genuine reason to exist, rather than simply being part of some endless process of squeezing more material out of a release. The occasion has to feel right, and so does the remixer. That’s why I’m quite selective about both. Mildreda hasn’t actually been through the remix machine that often, so having several artists reinterpret these songs was relatively new territory for Mildreda, and quite exciting. Das Ich were genuine heroes of my youth. Their first two albums still give me goosebumps today, and remarkably, they haven’t aged at all. They were simply light-years ahead of their time. Having Bruno remix one of my songs was therefore a childhood dream coming true. And when I first heard the result, I actually did a little dance of joy. It sounds unmistakably like Das Ich, yet “End of the Line” is still clearly there. In a strange way, it feels like a true hybrid: half my song, half a Das Ich composition. Perhaps that is also an answer to your question about where the identity of a song resides. Apparently you can change an enormous amount and still preserve some kind of core that remains recognisable. I’m equally happy with the other remixes. Steril are heroes of mine as well, and they transformed “End of the Line” into a wonderfully tight club track. Flesh Field, on the other hand, happened to cross my path at exactly the right moment, so involving him was almost an act of serendipity. I loved hearing “Virtual Goddess” thrown into his wonderfully mad industrial mixture of bombast, aggression and even a touch of dubstep. What fascinates me about all three is that I can still recognise my songs, but I’m hearing them through someone else’s ears. Maybe that’s what a good remix should do: not simply decorate the original, but reveal another possible reality that was somehow already hiding inside it. The Das Ich and Steril versions of “End of the Line” were released on the June 2026 EP, while the “Virtual Goddess” release includes the Flesh Field remix. Karo: “Virtual Goddess” avoids one of the easiest traps in writing about digital culture because the narrator is implicated in the mechanism he criticises. There is a virtual goddess, but there is also a virtual god; desire becomes entangled with images, attention, views and projection, so nobody gets to occupy the comfortable position outside the system. Is complicity important here? Have we reached a point where criticising mediated reality while continuing to produce, consume and emotionally invest in it is itself one of the defining contradictions of contemporary life? Jan: This is a difficult question because there are several things tangled up in it. There is the sheer amount of our day that social media consumes, but also the way it affects how we present ourselves and how we perceive other people. Both images are inevitably distorted. At the same time, however critical I am of social media, I can’t dismiss it as purely negative. It remains, whether we like it or not, an important way of discovering music and news, staying connected and sharing your own story with the world. And occasionally you even find a good joke there. So yes, complicity is absolutely part of it. I notice the contradiction in myself all the time. I can hardly keep away from my smartphone, call it an addiction if you like, while simultaneously being deeply irritated by the whole mechanism. I’m frustrated by all those pixel-perfect façades, yet at the same time I participate in creating one myself. I criticise the game while continuing to play it. And artificial intelligence is adding yet another layer of complexity to all of this. The boundaries between what is real, constructed, enhanced or entirely artificial are becoming increasingly difficult to define. We seem to be living inside a fascinating and slightly disturbing science-fiction film, except that none of us gets to sit outside it and simply watch. Karo: “Götterfall” almost feels like an older Mildreda argument surviving inside an entirely different philosophical environment. We have discussed your atheism before, and the quasi-sacral architecture of “Blue-Devilled” has largely vanished, yet somebody is still firing at gods who remain silent, mocking and apparently impossible to kill. If those gods are no longer theological, what has taken their place? Are there ideas, institutions, authorities, memories or even people we consciously stop believing in while continuing to grant them enormous psychological power? Jan: The ancient Greek historian Herodotus tells us that the Getae would shoot arrows into the sky during thunderstorms, threatening their god. I’ve always found that an incredibly powerful image, and I had actually used it before in a Your Life On Hold song. But it was simply too strong not to bring into the Mildreda universe as well: man, confronted with a reality he cannot accept, firing his arrows at the heavens. I also knew I wanted a song in German on the album, which allowed me to reshape the idea into something new. The arrows became bullets, and German inevitably gives the whole thing a very different weight and character. But the central idea remained the same: we are powerless and insignificant, raging against forces that are infinitely larger than ourselves. Karo: “Reality” widens the scope dramatically at the end: headlines, war, mediated violence, environmental destruction, the repeated consumption of catastrophe through screens. Much of the album has dealt with extremely intimate realities such as desire, damage, loneliness, ageing and unrealised possibilities, and then the individual is placed inside this enormous informational environment. Is the movement outward suggesting that there is ultimately no purely private reality, because even our most intimate emotional lives are continuously penetrated and reorganised by images, narratives and catastrophes arriving from outside? Jan: Despite what the title might suggest, this closing track is something of an outsider on the album in terms of content indeed. Where the rest of the album navigates my inner landscape, this song shifts its gaze to the world around me, our planet, and it isn’t doing well. Long-time fans who were with us back in the cassette days may recognise this piece. I wrote the first demo thirty years ago. I had always intended to give it a definitive version someday, and this album finally made that possible: new lyrics, new sound and a long-awaited rebirth. Karo: Finally, you already have concerts around the new-album period, including NCN in Deutzen on September 6 and Fourscher Festival in Erfurt in November. What happens after those dates? Are further Mildreda concerts already being discussed, and is the ambition eventually to take “Realities” on a more extensive tour of its own? Jan: I definitely hope to play a lot of shows with Mildreda in 2027. A few things have already been confirmed, but there’s still a lot up in the air. If the stars align, it could turn into quite an adventurous year! About Mildreda Mildreda is the Belgian dark-electro project led by producer, vocalist and songwriter Jan Dewulf. Its roots go back to the mid-1990s, when Dewulf, still in his teens and strongly affected by the cold Belgian electronics of acts such as The Klinik, began working with synthesizers and home-recording equipment. His self-released cassette “II Castrato” appeared in 1995, followed by “De Laffe Denker” in 1996. The latter circulated widely through the electro underground, and Mildreda subsequently shared stages with acts including Plastic Noise Experience, Terminal Choice, Covenant and VNV Nation. Dewulf later put Mildreda on hold and concentrated on Diskonnekted, while also completing a degree in philosophy. He returned to Mildreda with the digitally released “Coward Philosophy” in 2016. After signing with Dependent Records, the project released “I Was Never Really There” in 2021, bringing the early Belgian dark-electro foundations into a substantially more detailed contemporary production environment. Guests on that record included Dirk Ivens, Cyan of The Eternal Afflict and Numb’s Don Gordon, while Claus Larsen of Leaether Strip handled mastering. The concept album “Blue-Devilled” followed in December 2023. Built partly around Jean-Paul Sartre’s treatment of hell and the judgement of others, it expanded Mildreda’s melodic and atmospheric vocabulary while retaining its Belgian and Canadian dark-electro foundations. “Realities”, released on August 28, 2026 through Dependent, contains 18 tracks across two discs and is available as a limited 48-page hardcover artbook designed by Henk Willems. The album features Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada on “Rückwärts” and Johan Van Roy of Suicide Commando on “Virtual Goddess”. Its conceptual grounding shifts from Sartre towards Camus, while recurring “Reality Checks” connect the individual compositions into one continuous album structure. Mildreda’s official biography describes the project as led by Dewulf; the live incarnation consists of Jan Dewulf and Christophe “Salva” Salvatore. The single “Silk Skin” preceded the album in August 2026. Interview by Karo Kratochwil.

items.body: Chilean producer and composer Santiago Nicolás released “Atrición” on 18 August 2026, the first release under the solo alias he took from his own name, Santiago Nicolás González Lihn. The five-track EP is self-released, digital, and runs a little over 21 minutes. He composed, produced and mixed all of it. The tracklist runs “Todo Archivo Tiene una Grieta” (5:08), “Lo Primero Es la Contracción” (4:27), “Ensayo Continuo de Precisión” featuring Kimin Kim of the Korean band PCR (3:43), “No Todo lo que Arde Tiene que Morir” (5:15) and “Un Canto para el Herido” (2:48). Downloads are offered in MP3, FLAC and 24-bit/96 kHz at a name-your-price minimum of nine dollars. Two of those tracks appeared first as singles. “Ensayo Continuo de Precisión” went out on 28 May 2026 and “Lo Primero Es la Contracción” on 4 June 2026, both mastered by the producer at Estudios 6AM in Santiago. Atrición by Santiago Nicolás Where the Santiago Nicolás lyrics on ‘Atrición’ come from The words did not start as lyrics. They come from a series of poems written in the waiting room of an oncology centre, and the record sets that material against political violence, borders, archives and inherited trauma. The EP mixes hard, exact drum programming with the forward motion of contemporary techno, and the mix keeps every impact audible rather than smoothing it into texture. A physical edition is planned through the label Anything That Makes Light, collecting the poems alongside unreleased visual material, photographs and notes. It has not yet gone on sale, and no date has been given. About Santiago Nicolás Santiago Nicolás is the solo alias of Santiago Nicolás González Lihn, a producer, composer and artist based in Santiago, Chile. He has spent over a decade across electronic music, noise, experimental composition and post-punk, and opened the alias in May 2026. He records and has recorded under several other names. As Access Device he released a run of albums on Bandcamp between 2021 and 2023, among them “Detrás del Paisaje”, “Nueve Variables”, “Ceremonias” and “Ori. Gen” in 2021, “Luminiscencia” in 2022 and “Eón Codex” in 2023, working from Mexico City for part of that period. With filmmaker Pedro Roca he forms the Chilean duo Ángel de la Guarda, whose “Sentencia” appeared in June 2022, followed by “Crimen” the same year and “Alfanumérico” in 2023. His most recent band credit is The Deadly Affair, whose album “Visions Through The Sense of Silence” came out on 16 May 2025 through Anything That Makes Light. González Lihn wrote and composed every song on it and co-produced with Atom™, who also mixed and mastered the record; Diego Lorca played drums and Louise Schmidt Aguayo played bass and sang backing vocals. The Santiago Nicolás alias began releasing in May 2026 with the two singles that now sit inside “Atrición”. The EP is his first full release under the name.

items.body: Los Angeles industrial artist Staytus released the video for “Secret Hand” on 21 August 2026 through Cleopatra Records. Vicente Cordero directed it, his second video for the project after “S + M” in May 2026. The track is Staytus’ second release since signing to the label. Sam Grundemann, who records as Staytus, put the guitar and bass work at the centre of the track and described the video as a chance to perform it rather than illustrate it: “Secret Hand has some of my favorite guitar and bass work I’ve done. I wanted the music to feel just as seductive as it is dangerous – something that pulls you in before you realize how intense it has become. The video gave me the opportunity to fully embody that energy and step into this fearless, unapologetic version of myself as an artist.” Where Staytus recorded ‘Secret Hand’ The title is also the address. “Secret Hand” was recorded at Secret Hand Studios in Los Angeles, the room owned by drummer Jeff Friedl, whom Grundemann has worked with before. Cordero shot the video in a single black room streaked with neon and filled with fog, with the camera circling Grundemann throughout. Musically the track mixes hard guitar, bass and electronic pressure, with the arrangement kept open enough for individual hits to register. No album has been announced around the single. About Staytus Staytus is the solo project of Sam Grundemann, a musician, producer, songwriter and audio engineer born in Arizona and now based in the Los Angeles area. The project mixes industrial, electronic and nu-metal elements. Side-Line first covered the project in March 2022, when three tracks from the debut album appeared ahead of release. That album, “Disease Of The Mind”, arrived on 9 September 2022 with thirteen tracks, and the eleven-track “Wasteland Of Broken Hearts” followed on 27 October 2023, extended by a three-track bonus edition in November 2023. A run of singles followed: “Can You Hear Me?” in September 2024, “68 KILL” in October 2024, “Suburban Gothic” in February 2025, “King Knight” in April 2025 and Staytus closes Twisted Frames series with industrial single ‘How To Be A Serial Killer’ in May 2025. Staytus drops ‘Headache’ single produced by Sean Beavan (Nine Inch Nails, Marilyn Manson, Slayer) arrived on 17 July 2025 with Sean Beavan producing, then Staytus drops ‘Heart Attack’ single today, September 4, Staytus announces new single “Kiss N Tell” for October 23 and Staytus drops new single ‘The God, The Artist, & The Creator’ in December 2025. Collaborators across those releases include Matt McJunkins, Mikal Blue, Jeff Friedl, Anthony Laurie and Patrick “Embryo” Tapu. The label deal was reported in Staytus signs with Cleopatra Records and announces ‘S + M’ in May 2026, and the digital single “S + M” arrived on 29 May 2026 with a Cordero-directed video. “Secret Hand” is the project’s first new material since.

items.body: Baltimore electro-industrial duo Pygmy Children released “Proof in Lies” on 21 August 2026 through Re:Mission Entertainment. The digital single carries two versions of the track, a short mix running 4:37 and a long mix running 6:42, and is the lead single from the brothers’ forthcoming fifth studio album “Into The Silence”. Pete Roper wrote the words and music. He and his brother Brian Roper produced and mixed the single, Jeff Mortimer mastered it, and Brian Roper made the cover art. The download is offered in MP3, FLAC and 24-bit/44.1 kHz. The song began with a notebook rather than a session. Pete Roper described the starting point as a set of lyrics he had abandoned years earlier: “I rediscovered some old lyrics in a notebook for a track that had never fully materialized. I still remembered the original chord progression, so I rewrote the lyrics, recorded the initial drum tracks, and the project began to take shape.” Proof in Lies by Pygmy Children How Pygmy Children built the ‘Proof in Lies’ video The accompanying video sets live performance footage against public-domain animation produced in the 1940s, recut by the duo and layered with original visual effects. Pete Roper set out what the assembled imagery is about: “The imagery in the video challenges our blurred perception of the boundary between reality and fantasy as we move through life increasingly disconnected from one another, following established paths without question and becoming desensitized to experiences beyond ourselves. The social acceptance of violence as a form of entertainment also emerges as a recurring theme. Finally, the unanswered question of what the recurring mysterious character possesses invites deeper interpretation.” No release date has been announced for “Into The Silence”. About Pygmy Children Pygmy Children are an electro-industrial duo from Baltimore, Maryland, made up of brothers Pete and Brian Roper. Pete Roper started on drums at fifteen and played in a speed metal band; Brian Roper began remixing that material on tape decks, and the project grew out of those experiments. The duo issued the “Face Down” EP in 1993 and the album “Malignant” in 1994 through No Name No Slogan, then signed to Cleopatra Records in 1995 for “Deconstruct”. A fourth release, “Low Life Dream”, followed in 1998 through the German label Out Of Line, with production input from George of Urania. Output stopped after that, and Pete Roper stated around 2005 that the project was over. The duo returned in 2025 by signing to Re:Mission Entertainment. The single “I Have No Name” arrived on 29 August 2025 with remixes by Frontal Boundary and Slipjoint, as announced when Pygmy Children return with new album ‘Coincidental Strategies’, first single out August 29. The five-track Pygmy Children release ‘Signal Unknown’ single/EP followed on 17 October 2025 with reworkings by Fermion, Interface, Deekay and George Hagegeorge. The album “Coincidental Strategies” arrived on 24 October 2025 as a digital release and a limited-edition CD, the duo’s first physical edition since 1998. They also played an East Coast run billed as the Resurrection Tour alongside Mentallo & The Fixer. Alongside their own catalogue the pair have taken on remix work for other Re:Mission Entertainment acts, including tracks on Frontal Boundary’s “Faith” EP and the album “Failure”. “Proof in Lies” is their first release of 2026 and opens the run-up to “Into The Silence”.

items.body: Washington, D.C. darkwave duo 2DCAT released the four-track EP “We’re Here” on 21 August 2026 as a self-released digital edition, together with a video for the title track. The EP is credited to Johan Hauck and HAEZL, and downloads are offered in MP3, FLAC and 24-bit/44.1 kHz. The tracklist runs “We’re Here”, a Blue Rose edit of the 2024 single “Frames”, “Never Enough” and “Salvation Will Not Come”. No physical edition has been issued. We’re Here by 2DCAT Who is speaking on the 2DCAT track ‘We’re Here’ The title track is written from the point of view of the dead, addressing the living. Hauck was direct about how the lyric should be read, and about the reassurance in the chorus line “We’re here to remind you you’re never alone”: “We wouldn’t blame anyone for hearing this as hopeful. The gates being steeled, the door appearing, the path looking clear… that’s not hope. That’s dying. The dead are your guides because they’ve already made that walk.” HAEZL, an opera singer, delivers the vocal without theatrical menace. Hauck builds and fabricates the synthesizers heard on the track himself, and designs analogue instruments and FPGA-based hardware from scratch. The arrangement draws on early European synthpop and darkwave, with measured tempo and severe textures. The video keeps the frame near-black, with unstable light and coarse grain. “We’re Here” belongs to a run of recent singles pointing toward a next 2DCAT album, which has not yet been announced. About 2DCAT 2DCAT are a dark synthpop duo based in Washington, D.C., built around analogue synthesizers and drawing on synth music of the late 1970s and early 1980s. Johan Hauck handles synthesizers, drum machines and arrangements and has played in electro-industrial bands for around two decades. HAEZL sings and plays theremin, and has worked as a backing singer for The Beach Boys, Patti LaBelle, Cynthia Erivo, Renée Fleming and The Filharmonic, with television appearances on VH1, TLC and The Today Show. Guitarist Ulf has also appeared in the lineup. The project began releasing on Bandcamp in January 2019 with “Electric”, followed by “Summer, 1983” in April 2019 and “03:00” in September 2019. Three releases arrived in 2020: “Delaware is Burning” in February, “Modern Dystopia” in April and “Weeks Where Decades Happen” in November. “Fantastic Voyage” appeared in December 2022 and “Data Fusion” in September 2023. Seven releases followed in 2024: “The Darkest Hour” in March, “Love and Life (Part 2)” in April, “Falling Down” in May, “Take My Hand” in July, the set “Covers” in August, the single “Frames” in September and “Elegy” in November. “Covers” included a version of Allie X’s “Off With Her Tits”, reported at the time in 2DCAT cover Allie X track ‘Off With Her Tits’ – Out now. A remix collection followed in January 2025, “This is not for you.” in July 2025 and “Eat The Rich” in May 2026. Every release to date has come out without a label. The duo played their first German club dates in July 2026: Köln’s Club Volta on 24 July as part of the Echoes of Rebellion festival, Munich’s Theater Drehleier on 30 July and Leipzig’s Darkflower on 31 July. “We’re Here” is their first release since those shows.

It runs three tracks and just over nine minutes: the title track at 2:46, “Oszillation” at 3:16 and “Widerstand” at 3:00. Zbigniew F. and Jürgen W. record as Mottek87 in a downtown Duisburg apartment with the shutters closed. The two mix post-punk guitars, cold synths and programmed drums, with Jürgen W. singing in German. Their own release copy describes them as “two long-time friends from Duisburg telling stories from a region in transition”. Kleinkunst by Mottek87 What Mottek87 mean by ‘Kleinkunst’ The German title carries a double meaning: cabaret or variety performance on one reading, small art on the other. The duo set out what they wanted the word to do here: “Kleinkunst is about realizing that change is not automatically freedom.” They added a second line on the same point: “Sometimes something gets better, and you still need time to stop being angry about it.” Their Bandcamp page places that reading in a region undergoing structural change, which is the setting the duo have used since their first upload in January 2025. About Mottek87 Mottek87 are a post-punk duo from Duisburg in Germany’s Ruhr area, formed in 2024 by Zbigniew F. and Jürgen W., two long-time friends of Polish descent who decided to make a record after an evening of drinking beer and listening to records. Jürgen W. sings; the pair build their tracks from guitars, bass, programmed drums and sparse synthesizers, with lyrics in German. The project’s first upload was the track “Grausamkeit” on 6 January 2025, followed a month later by the album “Wir kaufen und verkaufen alles” on 7 February 2025. The single “YOGTZE” arrived on 3 August 2025, the album “Zadamy Chleba” on 28 November 2025, and “Duisburger Schule” on 10 April 2026. Every Mottek87 release has been self-released and digital-only, sold directly through Bandcamp at name-your-price. The duo have not signed to a label and have not announced live dates. “Kleinkunst” is their sixth release in nineteen months and their first since “Duisburger Schule” in April.

items.body: Swedish synthpop duo Page released the five-track EP “Ett Förslag” on Energy Rekords on 24 July 2026, in a CD edition of 200 copies in a gatefold cardboard sleeve. The digital version followed on 31 July. The EP holds two songs recorded in spring 2026, a 2026 version of an older track, a remix and a cover. Eddie Bengtsson wrote the music and words. Christer Hermodsson produced, and Jonas Karlsson supplied the artwork. What is on the Page EP ‘Ett Förslag’ The running order is “Ett förslag”, “Glizerstrahl”, “Om ett tag – Anymachine redux”, “Mia & Tom – 2026 Version” and “Ingenting som betyder någonting”. The first two are the new recordings. Track three is a rework by Anymachine, the project of Ulf Persson of Arachnophobia, of the title track of Page’s 2025 “Om ett tag” EP. The closing track is a cover by Compute, the Swedish producer Ulrika Mild, of a song from Page’s album “Inget motstånd”, which Energy Rekords issued on 3 October 2025. Compute has worked with Page before, remixing “Som ett skal 1” in 2013 and forming The Volt with Bengtsson for the 2016 album “Thirteen Men”. The CD is sold through Hot Stuff Mailorder and at Swedish shows. The EP is also on Spotify and Apple Music. Energy Rekords describes the title track as a candidate for a Page album due after the summer; no release date for that album has been announced. About Page Page formed in 1980 in Malmö around Eddie Bengtsson on vocals, synths and songwriting, Marina Schiptjenko on synths and Anders Eliasson on synths, vocals and songwriting, with Jan Adolfsson on synth drums in 1980 and 1981. Eliasson left in 1983. The debut single “Dansande man” came out on Eskimo in 1983 in an edition of 300 copies, followed by “Som skjuten ur en kanon” in 1986, “Blå fötter” in 1987 and “Som en vind” in 1989 on Accelerating Blue Fish. Energy Rekords collected the early material on a self-titled release in 1992 and issued “The Lost Tapes” in 1994. The first studio album, “Hallå! (Var tog månbasen vägen?)”, arrived the same year, with “Glad” in 1995. Schiptjenko left in 1996; Bengtsson carried the group through “Hur så?” in 1996 and “Helt nära” in 1998 before a farewell show at Kåren in Gothenburg on 1 April 2000. Bengtsson and Schiptjenko restarted the group in 2010 with the album “Nu”, which reached number 34 on the Swedish chart. “Hemma” followed on Wonderland in 2013, then “Det är ingen vacker värld men det råkar vara så det ser ut” in 2017, “Fakta för alla” in 2019 and the LP “Aska under mitt skinn” in 2020. Side-Line covered the 2018 EP “Start”, which carried an Apoptygma Berzerk remix, the 2021 EP “Aska” and the 2023 album “En ny våg”. The band’s back catalogue of early singles reached digital platforms in October 2021. Both members run projects outside the duo. Bengtsson has recorded as S.P.O.C.K with Alexander Hofman, as Sista Mannen På Jorden with Matts Wiberg since 1986, and in This Fish Needs A Bike and The Volt; he also reworked ten My God Damn Territory tracks for a vinyl release in 2016. Schiptjenko plays in Vacuum and in BWO. “Ett Förslag” is the pair’s second Energy Rekords EP in fifteen months, after “Om ett tag” in May 2025 and the album “Inget motstånd” in October 2025.

items.body: Swedish-Norwegian electronic pop duo The Sound Veil Society release their debut album “Things We Kept” on 11 September 2026 through Progress Productions. The record runs to eleven tracks and appears on CD with three bonus tracks, on a limited black and white splatter vinyl, on a MiniDisc edition capped at 50 copies worldwide, and digitally. Preorders are open. Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson started the project in 2024 and put out three singles before the album. The pair bring an electronic pop that pairs wide synth arrangements with melodic vocal lines and mid-tempo rhythms. Progress Productions describes the album as the delayed follow-through on that first single: “The wait has been long but ever since the band dropped their debutsingle “The River” they have been working hard […]” Formats and tracklist for The Sound Veil Society album ‘Things We Kept’ The eleven-track running order is “Another Day”, “The River”, “Fishmonger’s Boy”, “Nothing to Say”, “Hunger for Light”, “OK”, “Bound In Circles”, “Track Record”, “Voices (feat. KÅRP)”, “The Longing” and “Epilogue”. Swedish act KÅRP guests on “Voices”. Bjørn Marius Borg of Xenturion Prime added guitar and bass to “Hunger for Light”. The CD carries three extra tracks that rework the singles: “The River (Extended)”, “OK (Radio Edit)” and “Hunger for Light (Radio Edit)”. The MiniDisc holds one exclusive track of its own and is the format the label caps at 50 copies. All three physical editions are on preorder through the Progress Productions shop, which lists the vinyl at 299 Swedish kronor, the MiniDisc at 279 and the CD at 139. The digital album is on Bandcamp, where the eleven-track version went up for preorder on 5 August 2026. Things We Kept by The Sound Veil Society To open the preorder the label issued a video of “Nothing to Say” recorded at E-Only Festival in Leipzig on 13 March 2026, filmed by Alex Jung. About The Sound Veil Society The Sound Veil Society formed in 2024 around two musicians with long records in Nordic electronic pop. Erlend Eilertsen, from Tønsberg in Norway, runs Essence Of Mind and the cinematic project Lights A.M., and joined Xenturion Prime in 2024. Hans-Olof Mattsson, from Lysekil in Sweden, co-founded Code 64 in 2003, started Xenturion Prime roughly a decade later, and played in Essence Of Mind in its later years. The demo of “OK” was the first piece they wrote together. Their debut single “The River” arrived on Progress Productions on 24 April 2025, paired with an extended version. It carried them to the midnight slot at Nocturnal Culture Night in Deutzen on 5 September 2025, their first German show. “OK” followed on 22 August 2025 and “Hunger for Light” on 6 March 2026, both with extended mixes and both with official videos. In March 2026 the duo played the warm-up party of the fifteenth E-Only Festival at Stadtbad Leipzig, the show the new live video comes from. Progress Productions states the pair is already confirmed for several 2027 festivals, among them Eastside in Halle (Saale). Progress Productions, the Swedish label run by Torny Gottberg, has carried the duo from the first single onward and released all three preceding singles. Side-Line covered the label’s approach in a labels interview with Torny Gottberg. “Things We Kept” is the project’s first long-form release and its first physical release in any format.

items.body: Frankie Rose released the video for “Return To Dust” on 21 August 2026, the second single from her album “Hila”, which arrives on 18 September 2026 through Born Losers Records outside the EU and UK and through Night School Records in the EU and UK. The Brooklyn songwriter directed the clip herself. “Return To Dust” sets Rose’s vocal high in the mix against drum machines, synthesizers and reverbed guitar, with the low end carrying most of the weight. Rose explains the song as a description of searching for the dead while asleep, and of failing at it. “In my dreams I travel the cosmos and the astral realm looking for ones I’ve lost,” she stated. “But I’m a pretty bad receiver, and I am pretty sure I keep missing what they’re trying to tell me.” The video follows that idea literally. Rose floats through star fields and planetary vistas in a homemade montage, drifting rather than exploring, and the cosmic scenery stays low-budget rather than cinematic. Frankie Rose sets ‘Hila’ for 18 September Rose announced “Hila” on 23 June 2026 alongside the first single, “Cant Be Wrong”. She describes the album as built around bereavement and the way it distorts perception. “Hila. A record about loss,” she stated. “What persists beyond the range of ordinary perception? The place mourning keeps returning to – not quite transcendence, not quite doubt. The edge of what we can see.” Rose produced the record herself at her home studio, with Justin Welch of Elastica and Lush on drums. She recorded it after touring with The Jesus and Mary Chain and Swervedriver. Night School Records describes the album as drawing on the darkness of later Coil, the production weight of Skinny Puppy and the vocal treatments associated with Cocteau Twins, with Robin Guthrie style guitar work on “Shadow Twin”. Saxophone and digital synthesis run through “Rainman” and the title track. “Hila” runs ten tracks: “Olo”, “Cant Be Wrong”, “Return To Dust”, “Shadow Twin”, “Rainman”, “Hila”, “Manifest”, “Best Of Times”, “TV Star” and “Velvet Refrain”. Born Losers Records issues it on black vinyl, on clear vinyl with a green centre, on CD and digitally, with a vinyl and T-shirt bundle also listed. Night School Records handles the EU and UK editions. She was an original member of Vivian Girls and played drums in Crystal Stilts and in Dum Dum Girls before moving to her own material. items.body: Through these streets of piss and pain, through the heavens of palm and shame With a legacy of decay, and when all else fails, we make that mirror promise Melbourne’s Lothario sounds as though somebody left the rehearsal-room door open during a small electrical fire, and their latest single IOU takes that sense of danger somewhere tender. The lead single from the band’s EP has the clipped guitar drive and propulsion of Blitz’s New Age, but its engine is a promise between people who have seen each other wrecked, furious, exhausted, spiritually bankrupt, and still worth coming back for in the end. Annaliese Redlich sings where friendship has survived enough damage to become a private religion, built from favours remembered, wounds forgiven, and the knowledge that somebody showed up when everybody else disappeared. “IOU is a love song to self, and to those who have stuck by you through thick and thin,” says Redlich. “Shameless cinematic optimism after wallowing in the pit of despair. An anthem for the dawning of a new day, and pledge to keep going.” Punk has always loved survival, usually with the emotional subtlety of a brick through a pharmacy window – making it through another day can be messy, indebted work. IOU channels this chaos as linear guitars push against a pub-rock stomp sharpened into something wiry and menacing, while Redlich turns gratitude into a public declaration. There is love here with bruises on its knuckles and a tab it intends to settle. This reckless fellowship spills into Maria Cecelia Tedemalm’s black-and-white video, where a woman drives through the wrong side of town collecting passengers as though she runs an after-hours ministry for the permanently disreputable. She becomes an oracle of rock ’n’ roll spirit, guitars for a pulpit, anarchy in the gasoline. The high-contrast photography recalls a lost seventies rock film, carrying the candid electricity of Godlis photographing people outside CBGB before anybody knew which faces would become history. Watch the video for IOU below: Lothario’s IOU EP also widens Redlich’s method after earlier material was recorded largely alone in her bedroom. Elsa Birrel, Beth Lockhart, and Will Clifford now enter more deeply into the process, with Redlich’s brother Matt recording the sessions. “I’ve always been a deeply collaborative person, but Lothario’s inception marked a period of me going totally inward,” says Redlich. “A time when I kinda hid away and just let all this stuff pour out of me that had been building over a lifetime. I had so much to prove to myself and understand about my own process. It was immensely empowering but it leaves you nowhere to hide and no one to hide behind. In spite of how many men were automatically given credit for what I made.” Listen to IOU below and order the EP here. The European tour begins September 13 at Leffingeleuren in Leffinge, Belgium, and concludes October 10 at Funtastic in Benidorm, Spain. items.body: Even after all this time I still put you above the rest Yours is the silence That’s deadliest Some loves end cleanly; others keep a key to the room long after the door has slammed. Silence can become its own kind of conversation, filled with imagined replies, remembered jokes, and the stubborn belief that one day the phone might light up with a name you never stopped wanting to see. Moving on sounds simple until the past still feels unfinished. Hope survives on little: a song, a street, a photograph, the sense that timing once failed where feeling did not. We cling because possibility is easier to carry than finality, and because love rarely leaves when communication does. Romantic failure has always needed good transportation. Trains leave, elevators close, taxis disappear down avenues, and somewhere across town the person you still love is living an entire evening without knowing you are composing speeches to them in your head. New York City’s Bunny X (Abbi Gordon and Jenny Bates) understand this beautifully on the effervescent Even If We Don’t Talk, a sweetly obsessive slice of synth-driven pop from the New York duo’s third album, Love On A High Floor. The album places Gordon and Bates amid the glass-and-steel ambitions of 1980s Manhattan, where money climbed toward the clouds while romance remained vulnerable to busy signals, missed trains, bad timing, and plain cowardice. Here, the emotional problem is brutally familiar: communication has stopped, yet hope keeps finding loopholes. “This track was a latecomer in the writing process and almost didn’t make the final cut at all since album production was in the final stages by the time the idea for the song came about,” says Gordon. “Even If We Don’t Talk explores the lingering inability to move on from a past love and the hope that something might still happen.” That unresolved ache gets dressed for Friday night. A driving synthwave-meets-Italo Disco beat gives the song forward motion while Gordon and Bates sing with an earnestness recalling Madonna. Whitney Houston, Sheila E. and Sheena Easton, when pop could make romantic disaster feel perfectly reasonable beneath fluorescent lights. Their voices eventually tumble into a call-and-response outro that practically begs for roller skates, polished floors, and one more lap before somebody turns the lights on. Director Alice Teeple, with Bates helming the visual effects, carries that sensibility into a video partly filmed around New York’s Financial District, transforming crossed paths into romantic slapstick with a corporate-era sheen. “We wanted to make this look as authentically from the 80s as possible,” says Teeple. “I am a big fan of shows like Moonlighting and movies like 9-5, so I jumped at the chance to try my hand at that with Abbi and Jenny. I borrowed some ideas from The Twilight Zone and the Boomtown Rats video for Banana Republic, they brought a great Working Girl aesthetic to their style. I loved the idea of missed connections due to transit troubles, crossed wires, and rotten timing. In the end it all works out, though! We all need a lighthearted distraction from the troubles of our world right now, and we created a delightful little vignette together.” Perhaps that happy ending explains the song’s charm. Anyone can declare a romance finished; the dangerous part is secretly leaving the porch light on. Even If We Don’t Talk lives in that unreasonable interval, where silence still contains possibility and every missed connection carries the ridiculous promise of another chance. Watch below: New York City retrowave duo Bunny X released their third full-length album, Love on a High Floor, on August 14th via Aztec Records. The record is available digitally and through Bandcamp, with vinyl and CD editions offered through ElasticStage. Framed by the wealth, ambition, and vertiginous excess of 1980s Wall Street, Love on a High Floor places Bunny X high above Manhattan, where polished offices and skyline views conceal the compromises accumulating beneath the surface. The setting becomes an apt backdrop for songs concerned with adulthood, romantic expectation, and the uneasy distance between the life one imagines and the life that eventually takes shape. The album also revisits ideas introduced on Bunny X’s debut, Young & In Love, effectively catching up with its characters years later. Teenage innocence has given way to careers, complicated relationships, and the realization that youthful ambitions rarely survive adulthood unchanged. Across Love on a High Floor, Bunny X examine that reckoning alongside the seductive promise of the American Dream, tracing how aspiration can gradually become disenchantment once success, love, and security prove harder to define than they first appeared. items.body: A slimmed down couple of weeks of posting continues here what with Alex being off at Infest getting to bug out to Utah Saints and the like, but back home at the HQ the arrival of the anniversary vinyl edition of Forma Tadre’s masterpiece Navigator has been, ahem, something good. While ID:UD’s main remit remains coverage of new releases within the broader world of Our Thing, taking time out to reflect on and enjoy something as classic and replayable as Navigator is always worthwhile (and hey, our commentary podcast on it is nearly a decade old to boot). On with the new stuff… Skren MRDTC, “Kommen (Unhuman)” We’re still making our way through the slew of archival releases underrated EBM experimentalists Divider dropped on Bandcamp a few months back, and now there’s an equally sizable morass of beats and basslines from German fellow travellers MRDTC which has just gone up on BC. It’s a bit difficult to ferret out what’s what but it looks as though the Kommen single (or “standalone concept EP” as the band term it, indicating variations on a theme rather than a traditional remix single, but who’s counting) is the new release from the duo, and its mix of murk and expertly sequenced beats makes for a solid introduction to the group and an invitation to go ham with the PWYW back catalog. Kommen by MRDTC Ortrotasce, “Not Mine” Each new release from Ortrotasce is a stylistic roll of the dice, and their latest single draws just about all of the moods Nic Hamersly’s work cycles through in a tight and elegantly minimal package. The throwback body music style’s right up front of course, but Ortrotasce’s ear for synthpop and minimal wave is still fully in play. Not Mine by Ortrotasce Skren, “Asphalt” Germany’s Skren have drawn our attention over the past couple of years by cogently picking up where aggrotech acts of preceding (harsh) generations left off while imbuing the classic sound with fresh energy. They’re clearly taking a page from modern dark techno on this new original track from their new remix release, yet are completely detouring around the modern TBM template for the sake of holding to the style’s connections to gabber and hardcore. ERROR_ by SKREN Odonis Odonis, “Yeah Whatever” Lastly, some proper CanCon game recognizing CanCon game for you. Not sure how we missed this earlier in the year, but Toronto machinists Odonis Odonis did right by one of Nettwerk’s most mercurial acts, Moev. The Yeah Whatever album at large remains a high watermark for a style which drew together fans of new wave and industrial, and the title track’s mix of languid harmonies and tight rhythms proved to be good and satisfying grist for Odonis Odonis’ steely mill. items.body: Sarah Davachi has topped our year-end chart twice, in 2018 and 2022 ~ sonically and mathematically, this may be her year yet again. Ambitious, immersive and enveloping, The Will of Tongues seems like the natural successor to Two Sisters, despite the fact that other albums have been released in-between. One of the reasons Davachi’s music resonates deeply with our readers and staff is that it lines up perfectly with our ethos. The new album “seeks to articulate a deep reverence for the act of listening,” Clocking in at 140 minutes, it’s neither a brief nor an easy listen, but the experience is intensely rewarding, especially on repeat plays. On first play, the surface appeal is audible: reverent organ, sumptuous strings, striving choir. On second play, the set creates a mood: active calm, heart and mind settled, the peace that passes understanding. But after this, the music turns transportive, a minor miracle one does not hear coming. At this point, the music passes through the body like blood and breath. The imagination is sparked, as if a stopgap has been unplugged. Suddenly there is access to the Divine. At this point, The Will of Tongues becomes more than the sum of its parts; it becomes a vehicle for transportation, with the suggestion of transmigration. The first phase includes an appreciation for the technical aspects of the work. Davachi performs on historic pipe organs in three nations, and enlists the aid of various ensembles: The Sung Blood Players (Whitney Johnson, Eyvind Kang and Lucy Railton, all familiar to our site), Renaissance flute consort Phaedrus, brass ensemble Diapson and Chamber Choir Ireland. The elaborate liner notes explore the background of the recordings and the players. In these pages, one may learn all about “vertical harmony, intervallic affect, canonic structure” and more, enough to fill a doctoral thesis as one examines the architecture of the compositions. But while these may lead to appreciation and admiration, they are only the starting basis of the set. The second phase includes the videos, as well as how one feels while watching the images. “Song of the Smile’s Fig: III. Follies” is a rare 45-length work from Davachi, five minutes of reflective choir. The video begins with a flower set against a purple sky, the camera shaking ever so slightly as the sun strikes the buds; and then a shift to evening, a black and white forest, a cabin, a foraging buck. Then the same forest in winter, candles attached to a rotating mechanism, a curtain opening and a table beckoning. Suggestion is more important here than elaboration. “Interlude V: Harmonic, for Woodwinds” is more abstract, beginning with a paint brush, setting lines and geometric shapes in deliberate motion until they become a lattice. “Canto Solo” introduces hues of cyanotype blue, a pair of cat’s eyes, a furtive hand over water and finally rapid interplay between color and black and white, Dicky Bahto’s work reminiscent of Underworld’s “Cowgirl” (Jemar Yusuf, director). The senses have been engaged, but the third eye has not yet been unlocked. For this one needs the music, and only the music. The album begins with an interlude: “Polyphonic, for Strings,” the first brick on the path to surrender. First the mind is free to wander; soon, it begins to settle on its own images and thoughts; eventually it drifts to higher subjects and deeper understandings, dissolving the constraints of time, widening one’s attitude toward humanity, cracking open the darkness so that the light may come in. For this reason, we recommend that one view the videos as points of entry, but not watch them so often that one associates the images with the sounds. From here, it is only a slight shift to “Canto Duo,” which swirls and flows and recedes; then “Song of the Smile’s Fig: I. Hours,” each piece revealing a different facet of the whole. The interrelated timbres of soloist and ensembles begin to produce a cumulative effect that requires time for full activation. In a spiritual sense, this is akin to the difference between a quick, rote prayer and the practice of prayer, between a church service and a spiritual retreat. In secular terms, the album imitates the runner’s high: one must push through and press on in order to enter a higher plane. Once one is fully immersed, one may begin to experience visions, or revelations, or at the very least an otherworldly calm. The Will of Tongues uses deep intervals to prompt deep encounters. The elements accumulate like grains of sand, or the rungs on Jacob’s Ladder. Davachi’s atmospheres clear a space for the Divine to enter and to be perceived, ultimately transcending the album as album, suggesting the music as a pathway, a portal, an open door. (Richard Allen)
